hook: Exabytes of photos, thousands of machines, and any one of them can die right now. How do the files survive?
title: Turning thousands of dying servers into one pool of files
body: A 1-billion-user app stores exabytes of photos and logs. No single machine can hold that, and any machine can die at any moment. A **distributed file system** (DFS) solves both problems at once. It spreads each file across many machines, keeps enough redundancy to survive disk, host and rack failures, and repairs itself when something breaks. Programs see none of this. They get a simple file path instead of a list of machines.
takeaway: Hide a thousand failing machines behind one file path.
deeper:
**Where it sits:** The DFS sits at the bottom of almost every big company's storage stack. Databases, blob stores and analytics engines are built on top of it, so its behavior leaks upward into everything else.

**Four duties, four problems:** Spreading files means tracking where every piece lives. Redundancy means choosing between full copies (replication) and cheaper coded fragments (erasure coding). Self-repair means background processes must notice a dead disk and rebuild what it held without paging a human. A simple path means clients never learn that a file is scattered across many servers in several racks.

**The hidden dataset:** Every duty creates bookkeeping. Which bytes are where, which copies are stale, which files exist: that is itself a large, fast-changing dataset. The bookkeeping, not the bytes, is the hard part. Every DFS from GFS in 2003 to Tectonic in 2021 is a different answer to how to keep it.

quiz.q: A startup keeps all user photos on two huge RAID servers. It grows to a billion users. Name the two walls it hits.
quiz.a: Capacity: no single machine can hold exabytes. Failure: any machine can die at any moment, so data must be spread across many machines with redundancy and automatic repair.

mcq.q: What does an application use to read a file stored in a DFS?
options: A simple file path, with placement hidden
A list of servers holding each block
The IDs of the disks storing each replica
A rack map it queries before each read
mcq.why: The DFS hides spreading, redundancy and repair. Programs get a simple file path instead of a list of machines.

hook: Double the storage servers and you nearly double capacity and throughput. So what still hits a wall?
title: Every DFS has two halves, and only one is hard
body: Adding storage servers to a distributed file system adds capacity and throughput almost linearly. That is the **data path**: storing and serving the actual bytes. The wall is elsewhere. The **metadata path** holds the namespace (directories and file names), the mapping from files to blocks, and the mapping from blocks to machines. Every open, create, list and rename touches it, and it has to stay consistent while the bytes fan out across thousands of machines.
takeaway: Bytes are independent; names are shared. That is why metadata is the hard half.
deeper:
**Why bytes scale:** Blocks of different files are independent. Two clients reading different blocks never coordinate, so you add servers and spread load without anyone talking to anyone.

**Why names don't:** The namespace is one shared tree. Creating a file must check the name is free. Renaming a directory changes the path of everything under it. Listing a directory needs a consistent view. The block map must agree with what servers actually hold. All of this needs ordering, and every client touches it on every file operation.

**The growth trap:** Metadata grows with the number of files, not bytes. A billion small files means a billion namespace entries even if the total data is modest. So when you review any storage system, find the metadata first. Many outages that look like data outages are really metadata outages.

quiz.q: A team adds 500 storage servers to a struggling DFS, but file creates and renames stay just as slow. Why didn't the new servers help?
quiz.a: Storage servers scale the data path. Creates and renames hit the metadata path, a shared namespace that needs coordination, so more storage servers add no metadata capacity.

mcq.q: Why does a DFS data path scale almost linearly with added servers?
options: Blocks of different files need no coordination
Each server keeps a full copy of the namespace
Clients batch small writes into larger requests
Replication spreads every read across all servers
mcq.why: Bytes of different files are independent, so new servers add capacity and throughput without adding coordination.

hook: GFS, HDFS, Colossus, Tectonic, Ceph. Two decades of file systems, all answering one question. Which one?
title: Two decades of DFS designs, one question
body: Every generation of distributed file system is a new answer to one question: how do we scale **metadata**? GFS put it in the RAM of one machine. HDFS copied that, then added federation and read replicas. Colossus and Tectonic moved metadata into a distributed database. Ceph removed part of it entirely by computing placement with a formula instead of storing it.
takeaway: Find where a system keeps its metadata, and you have found its ceiling.
deeper:
**Each fix, a new limit:** One in-memory master (GFS, early HDFS) gives simple code and strong semantics but runs out of RAM, CPU and recovery time. Federation splits the tree across masters, but hot directories stay hot. Read replicas offload reads, most of the traffic, yet writes still hit one node.

**Going further:** A distributed database (Bigtable under Colossus, ZippyDB under Tectonic) scales to billions of files, but cross-shard operations like rename get hard. Ceph's CRUSH has no block-location table at all, but data moves whenever the cluster map changes.

**What stays constant:** The data path barely changes. Clients still learn where bytes live, then talk directly to storage servers. What changes is who knows where the bytes live, and how that knowledge is stored, split and recovered. Read each system through that lens and you can predict its limits before reading its failure stories.

quiz.q: A vendor pitches a new DFS that "scales without limit". What one question cuts through the pitch, and which answers should worry you?
quiz.a: Where does the metadata live and how does it grow? One in-memory server means RAM, CPU and recovery limits; static splits mean hot directories; a sharded database means hard cross-shard renames.

mcq.q: How did Ceph shrink its metadata problem?
options: It computes placement with a formula
It stores metadata in Bigtable
It keeps all metadata in one server's RAM
It adds read replicas of one master
mcq.why: Ceph's CRUSH computes where data lives, so there is no stored block-location table to scale.

hook: Why would a file system pick 64 MB chunks and let records land twice? Blame five bets made in 2003.
title: GFS bet that hardware fails constantly, and built for it
body: The GFS paper (SOSP 2003) started from assumptions that were unusual at the time. Component failures are the norm on cheap **commodity machines**. Files are huge. Most writes are appends, and most reads are large streams. Sustained bandwidth matters more than latency. Many clients may append to the same file at once. These fit Google's early crawl, indexing and MapReduce workloads, and they explain every design choice that follows.
takeaway: Write your workload assumptions down. They decide what your system will be bad at.
deeper:
**Assumption to feature:** Huge files justify huge 64 MB chunks. Append-heavy writes justify a special record append instead of optimizing random overwrites. Bandwidth over latency justifies pushing data along chains of servers to use full network bandwidth. Many concurrent appenders justify relaxed consistency, where GFS picks the offset and applications handle duplicates.

**Failure as routine:** If failures are the norm, detection and repair must be built in, not bolted on. Hence heartbeats from every chunkserver, 3 replicas per chunk by default, and automatic re-replication.

**The catch:** A design that fits its original workload this well fits others poorly. When Google later needed latency-sensitive services and billions of small files, the same assumptions became the limits. The assumptions you never write down are the ones that ambush you later.

quiz.q: You need 5 ms reads across millions of 10 KB files. Why is a GFS-style design a poor fit?
quiz.a: GFS assumed huge files, large streaming reads and bandwidth over latency. Its 64 MB chunks, single master and batch-oriented design do not suit latency-sensitive small-file workloads.

mcq.q: Which workloads did GFS's original assumptions fit?
options: Crawl, indexing and MapReduce batch jobs
Low-latency serving of small user files
Random overwrites of database pages
POSIX home directories for developers
mcq.why: GFS assumed huge files, appends, large streaming reads and bandwidth over latency, which matched Google's crawl, indexing and MapReduce.

hook: One machine knows every file name. The rest hold bytes and know nothing about files. How does a read work?
title: One master, many chunkservers, 64 MB chunks
body: A GFS cluster has one **master** and many **chunkservers**. Files are split into fixed 64 MB chunks, each with a globally unique 64-bit chunk handle. Chunkservers store chunks as ordinary Linux files and know nothing about directories. Each chunk lives on 3 chunkservers by default. To read, the client library turns a file name and offset into a chunk index, asks the master for the handle and replica locations, then reads from a chunkserver directly.
takeaway: Split who knows from who stores, and each side can stay simple.
deeper:
**Sharp division:** The master knows the namespace, which chunks make up each file, and where each chunk's replicas live. Chunkservers store chunk-sized Linux files and answer reads and writes. The master exchanges heartbeats and instructions with them, which is how it learns their state.

**Plain files underneath:** Storing chunks as ordinary Linux files was pragmatic. The local file system handles space allocation and disk layout. GFS adds only distribution, replication and naming on top.

**Why this shape:** Three-way replication on cheap machines gave durability without special hardware, fitting the assumption that failures are constant. One master made the system simple to build and reason about. That same master would later become the main limit, but in 2003 the simplicity was worth it.

quiz.q: An engineer logs into a GFS chunkserver and lists the files on its disk. What do they find, and what can't they learn from it?
quiz.a: Ordinary Linux files, one per chunk. They can't tell which GFS file or directory a chunk belongs to; only the master holds the namespace and the file-to-chunk map.

mcq.q: What are GFS's default chunk size and replication?
options: 64 MB chunks on 3 chunkservers
128 MB chunks on 3 chunkservers
64 MB chunks on 2 chunkservers
1 GB chunks on 3 chunkservers
mcq.why: GFS chunks are 64 MB with a 64-bit handle, replicated on 3 chunkservers by default. 128 MB is HDFS; 1 GB is Azure's extent size.

hook: One GFS machine kept the whole cluster's metadata in RAM. So what stopped a crash from wiping it out?
title: The GFS master lives in RAM and survives on a log
body: Keeping all metadata in memory made the GFS master fast: the namespace, the file-to-chunk map and every replica's location. It needed less than 64 bytes per 64 MB chunk. But RAM vanishes on a crash. So every namespace change goes to an **operation log**, replicated to remote machines. Periodic **checkpoints** keep recovery fast: load the latest snapshot, then replay only the log written after it.
takeaway: Memory for speed, a replicated log for truth.
deeper:
**Why RAM worked:** At under 64 bytes per 64 MB chunk, 1 PB is about 16 million chunks, so about 1 GB of master RAM for chunk metadata. In-memory state also lets the master scan everything quickly for background work.

**Why the log matters:** A namespace change counts only once its log record is written locally and on remote replicas, so a crash cannot lose a completed operation. Checkpoints bound recovery, because replaying years of records from the start would take far too long.

**The catch:** Recovery still takes real time. The master loads the checkpoint and replays the log, and writes stop meanwhile. That window, along with RAM for file names and one machine's CPU, is part of why GFS hit a ceiling. Simplicity and speed now, a known limit later.

quiz.q: A GFS-style master logs every change for years but never takes a checkpoint. Then it reboots. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Recovery must replay the entire log from the beginning, which takes far too long, and writes stop until it finishes. Checkpoints let it load a snapshot and replay only recent records.

mcq.q: How does the GFS master avoid losing namespace changes in a crash?
options: It logs them to replicated remote machines
It asks chunkservers to report the namespace
It keeps a copy in every client's cache
It writes metadata inside every chunk
mcq.why: Namespace changes go to an operation log replicated on remote machines, with checkpoints so recovery replays only recent records.

hook: The GFS master is the one machine that knows where every chunk lives, yet it never writes that down. Why?
title: The GFS master never saves where chunks live
body: In a GFS cluster, disks fail, chunkservers restart and machines come and go all the time. A stored list of chunk locations would drift from reality with every change. So the master does not persist chunk locations at all. It learns them from chunkservers at startup and through regular heartbeats. The chunkserver is the **source of truth** for what it holds, so the master's view never drifts out of sync.
takeaway: Let whoever physically holds a fact be the authority for it.
deeper:
**The alternative fails:** If the master stored locations, every disk failure, replacement and restart would need a coordinated update. Miss one, and the master believes a replica exists when it does not. With failures as the norm, that disagreement would be routine.

**What it does persist:** The operation log covers only what the master alone decides: the namespace and the file-to-chunk mapping. Everything physical is rebuilt from what chunkservers report.

**The catch at scale:** HDFS copied the idea, with DataNodes sending block reports to the NameNode. But reports from thousands of nodes are a big RPC load on one process, one reason NameNode RPC throughput later became a limit. Asking is cheaper than remembering, until thousands of servers answer at once.

quiz.q: A GFS chunkserver's disk dies overnight and no one updates any record. Why doesn't the master keep sending clients to the dead replicas?
quiz.a: The master never stored those locations. It rebuilds them from chunkserver reports and heartbeats, and the failed disk's chunks stop being reported, so its view follows reality.

mcq.q: Where does a restarted GFS master get chunk replica locations?
options: From chunkserver reports at startup
From its replicated operation log
From its latest checkpoint file
From client caches of recent lookups
mcq.why: Locations are never persisted. Chunkservers are the source of truth and report their chunks at startup and through heartbeats.

predict.q: The GFS master persists its metadata in an operation log. Which piece does it deliberately never save?
options: Where each chunk's replicas live
The mapping from files to chunks
The directory and file names

hook: Hundreds of clients shared one GFS master in 2003. Why didn't every read queue up behind it?
title: GFS clients never read file data through the master
body: One master serving every byte to many clients would choke its CPU and network card. GFS avoids that by keeping data off the master entirely. Clients ask where a chunk lives, **cache** the answer, and then talk directly to chunkservers for the bytes. The master handles only small metadata requests. The heavy traffic spreads across the chunkservers, and a cached location lets later reads skip the master altogether.
takeaway: The master gives directions. It never carries the bytes.
deeper:
**A pattern everyone copied:** Separating the lookup from the transfer shows up in every later system. Colossus clients talk to curators for control operations and move data directly with D file servers. HDFS clients get block locations from the NameNode and stream from DataNodes. Lustre clients get a layout from the metadata target, then read many object storage targets directly.

**Caching multiplies it:** A chunk's location rarely changes, so one answer serves many reads.

**The catch:** Caching helps only once a client knows a file. Opening, creating, listing and deleting still go to the master. When thousands of MapReduce tasks open files at once, those calls pile up on one machine. Keeping data off the master was necessary but not sufficient: the metadata operation rate became the next bottleneck.

quiz.q: A GFS master's network card is saturated. A teammate blames a batch job streaming terabytes. Why is that unlikely, and what's the likelier cause?
quiz.a: File bytes never pass through the master. More likely many tasks are opening, creating or listing files at once, flooding it with metadata requests.

mcq.q: What traffic does the GFS master handle?
options: Small metadata lookups only
All reads, but no writes
All writes, but no reads
Every byte of small files
mcq.why: Clients get chunk locations from the master, cache them, and move all file data directly with chunkservers.

hook: Huge chunks saved GFS master RAM. Then one small program, launched on hundreds of machines, exposed the cost.
title: Why 64 MB chunks turned small files into hot spots
body: GFS picked 64 MB chunks, huge by file system standards. Fewer chunks mean less master RAM and fewer client-to-master calls, since one lookup covers a big range of a file. The cost lands on small files. A small file is a single chunk, so it lives on only a few chunkservers. When an executable stored in GFS was started on hundreds of machines at once, those few chunkservers became **hot spots**.
takeaway: Chunk size trades metadata cost against how widely load can spread.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** Master memory and lookup traffic scale with the number of chunks. At 64 MB per chunk and under 64 bytes of metadata each, 1 PB is about 16 million chunks and roughly 1 GB of master RAM.

**Granularity mismatch:** A popular large file spreads its readers over many chunks, so many servers share the load. A popular small file can't. Every reader converges on the handful of replicas that hold its single chunk. Bigger chunks make metadata cheaper and small popular files hotter, in the same move.

**Other choices:** HDFS uses 128 MB blocks. Azure packs many small objects into 1 GB extents and keeps a separate index for the objects, so its bottom layer tracks few, big units.

quiz.q: 5,000 servers read a 2 MB config file at boot; the same 5,000 read a 50 GB dataset. Both live in GFS. Which read suffers, and why?
quiz.a: The config file. It is one chunk on about 3 chunkservers, so all 5,000 readers hit them. The dataset spans hundreds of chunks, spreading readers across many servers.

mcq.q: Why did GFS choose large 64 MB chunks?
options: Less master RAM and fewer lookups
Faster random writes inside files
Better load spreading for small files
Simpler erasure coding across racks
mcq.why: Master memory and client-master calls scale with chunk count, so bigger chunks shrink both. The price is hot spots on small popular files.

predict.q: An executable stored in GFS is started on hundreds of machines at once. What goes wrong?
options: Its few chunkservers become hot spots
The master runs out of RAM
The file's replicas diverge

hook: Three copies of the same chunk receive writes at the same moment. Who decides which write came first?
title: How GFS keeps 3 replicas writing in the same order
body: If each replica picked its own order, your three copies would quietly drift apart. GFS answers with a **lease**. The master gives one replica, the **primary**, temporary authority over a chunk: an initial 60-second timeout, extended while writes keep coming. The primary assigns a serial order to every write, and the secondaries apply writes in exactly that order. The master never touches individual writes. It decides only who is in charge, and for how long.
takeaway: Centralize the rare decision (who leads). Delegate the frequent one (what order).
deeper:
**Why a timeout:** Why not let a lease last until the master revokes it? Because the primary can crash or become unreachable, and a master that must reach a replica to take back its authority is stuck. With a timeout, the master just waits for the lease to run out, then grants a new one elsewhere.

**Never two bosses:** The old lease must expire before a new one is issued, so there are never two primaries, and the silent replica never has to cooperate. Extensions keep a busy chunk's primary stable. Failure is handled by the clock, not by a conversation with a dead machine.

**Load stays low:** The master's job shrinks to granting and extending leases on chunks being written. The high-frequency ordering work lives on the primaries.

quiz.q: A GFS primary goes silent. It might be dead or just cut off. Why can the master safely appoint a new primary without hearing back from it?
quiz.a: It waits for the old lease to expire. After that the old primary has no authority, so two primaries never overlap and the silent replica's cooperation is not needed.

mcq.q: How long does a GFS chunk lease last?
options: 60 seconds, extended while writes continue
15 minutes, matching delayed recovery
60 seconds, and never extended
Until the master explicitly revokes it
mcq.why: A lease starts with a 60-second timeout and is extended while writes continue. Expiry lets the master replace a failed primary safely.

hook: GFS copies a write to 3 replicas in roughly the time it takes to send one copy. How?
title: GFS moves the bytes first, the write command second
body: GFS splits a write into two paths. First the client pushes the data along a **chain** of chunkservers, each forwarding to the next closest one, so every machine uses its full network bandwidth. Only after all replicas hold the data does the client send the write request to the primary. The primary assigns a serial number and applies the write, the secondaries follow that order, and the primary reports success or error.
takeaway: Bytes follow the network. Order follows the primary.
deeper:
**Why a chain:** If the client sent all three copies, its outbound link would be split three ways. In a chain, each machine spends its full outbound bandwidth forwarding to the next, so replication costs about one transfer plus small pipeline delays. Picking the next closest machine keeps cross-rack traffic low.

**The full sequence:**
1. Client asks the master who holds the lease.
2. Master returns primary and secondary locations.
3. Client pushes data; replicas forward it along the chain.
4. Client sends the write request to the primary.
5. Primary orders and applies it; secondaries follow and report done.

**Why decouple:** The heavy part can take whatever path is best for bandwidth, while ordering stays with the primary regardless of topology. Colossus, Tectonic and HDFS all keep bytes and control on separate paths.

quiz.q: A client in rack A writes to replicas in racks A, B and B. Why push the data A to B to B instead of from the client to all three?
quiz.a: The client's outbound link isn't split three ways. Each hop uses its full bandwidth forwarding to the next closest machine, and the data crosses racks only once.

mcq.q: When does a GFS client send the write request to the primary?
options: After every replica has received the data
Before any data is pushed to replicas
In parallel with the first data transfer
After the secondaries have applied it
mcq.why: Data flows first along the chain. The control request goes to the primary only once every replica holds the data.

hook: A chunkserver returns after missing writes and reports its chunks as usual. How does GFS spot the stale ones?
title: One counter per chunk exposes replicas that missed writes
body: A replica that missed writes while its chunkserver was down looks, in its own report, exactly like a healthy one. GFS catches it with a **chunk version number**. The master increases a chunk's version each time it grants a new lease, and the replicas taking part record it. A replica that was down keeps the old number. When its chunkserver returns and reports, the lower version marks it as a **stale replica**.
takeaway: Bump a number at every change of authority. Absentees can't fake it.
deeper:
**Why at lease time:** A new lease marks the start of a new round of writes, so it is the natural moment to bump the version. Every replica that takes part learns the new number. One on a dead machine cannot.

**How it's used:** Chunkservers report their chunks and versions at startup and in heartbeats. The master compares each against its own record. Stale replicas are not handed to clients as valid locations, and good copies are re-replicated to restore the replication factor.

**Why it's needed:** The master learns locations from chunkservers instead of storing them. Without versions, a returning server's report would be indistinguishable from a healthy replica, and clients might read old data. Epoch numbers like this are a standard way to reject state from anyone absent during a change.

quiz.q: Chunk X is at version 7. One chunkserver holding X crashes, the master grants a new lease, and writes continue. The server returns reporting version 7. What happens?
quiz.a: The master's record says 8, so that replica is stale. It is not given to clients, and the chunk is re-replicated from up-to-date copies.

mcq.q: When does the GFS master increase a chunk's version number?
options: Each time it grants a new lease
After every write to the chunk
On every chunkserver heartbeat
Whenever the chunk is re-replicated
mcq.why: Tying the bump to new leases means a replica absent for that grant keeps an older version and shows up as stale.

hook: Many writers, one file, zero locks between them. GFS made it work, with a catch in the fine print.
title: Record append: GFS picks the offset, lands it at least once
body: Many producers writing into one file would normally need locks to agree on offsets. GFS added **record append** instead. The client supplies only the data. GFS appends it atomically at least once, at an offset it chooses, and returns that offset. The catch is "at least once". If an append fails on one replica, the client retries, and the retry lands at a new offset. Some replicas may then hold the record twice, or padding or partial garbage in the failed region.
takeaway: "At least once" means "sometimes twice". Build readers that expect it.
deeper:
**Who picks the offset:** The primary already orders all writes to the chunk, so it chooses the offset and the secondaries follow. No producer coordinates with any other, which suits many clients appending to the same file at once.

**What a retry leaves:** Say one secondary fails. The client sees an error and retries the whole append. Replicas that wrote the first attempt keep it. After the retry succeeds at a new offset, those replicas hold the record twice, while the failed replica has garbage or padding in that range.

**The guarantee, exactly:** Each record lands atomically, at least once, at an offset GFS chose. The file is not promised to be byte-identical across replicas. Cleaning up the leftovers was the application's job.

quiz.q: Your log collector writes events with GFS record append and counts them by counting records. The totals come out slightly high. Why, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: Failed appends are retried at new offsets, so some records appear twice. Give each record a unique ID and drop duplicates on read, with checksums to skip padding.

mcq.q: What does a GFS client provide in a record append?
options: Only the data; GFS chooses the offset
The data and the exact file offset
A lock token along with the data
The data and a target replica
mcq.why: Record append takes only data. GFS picks the offset, appends atomically at least once, and returns the offset.

predict.q: A GFS record append succeeds on two replicas and fails on the third. The client retries and succeeds. What can the first two replicas now hold?
options: The record twice
The record once, as usual
Nothing: the first attempt rolls back

hook: Every replica returns the exact same bytes, and the data is still wrong. GFS has a word for that.
title: Consistent is not defined: GFS's two-word guarantee
body: Replicas agreeing and data making sense are different promises, and GFS names both. A region is **consistent** if all clients see the same data from any replica. It is **defined** if it is consistent and clients see exactly what one mutation wrote. Successful serial writes leave a region defined. Concurrent successful writes leave it consistent but undefined: mixed fragments. A failed write leaves it inconsistent. Record append gives defined records, possibly with inconsistent regions between them.
takeaway: Replicas can agree perfectly on bytes nobody wrote.
deeper:
**Consistent, undefined:** Two clients overwrite the same large range at once. Their writes may be split into chunk-sized operations, and the primary may interleave pieces of both. Every replica applies the same interleaving, so all readers see the same bytes. But those bytes are a patchwork no single client wrote.

**Inconsistent:** A failed write is worse. Some replicas applied it and some did not, so the answer depends on which replica you hit.

**Record append in between:** Each successful record is defined, an intact copy of one client's data. The regions around it may hold padding, failed fragments or duplicates that differ by replica.

**Why the words matter:** Many systems blur replica agreement and write atomicity. They are separate guarantees, and a system can give one without the other.

quiz.q: Two GFS clients overwrite the same 200 MB range at the same moment and both succeed. A reader checks all 3 replicas. What does it see?
quiz.a: The same bytes on every replica (consistent), but a mix of fragments from both writers (undefined), because large writes split into pieces the primary may interleave.

mcq.q: What state does a failed GFS write leave a region in?
options: Inconsistent: replicas may differ
Consistent but undefined: fragments mix
Defined: one writer's data intact
Defined, with padding at the end
mcq.why: Some replicas applied the failed write and some did not, so readers can see different data depending on the replica.

hook: GFS made concurrent appends fast and simple. Every application reading those files paid for it. How?
title: GFS's relaxed consistency became every app's problem
body: Record append could leave duplicates, padding and partial garbage in a file. GFS didn't clean that up. Applications did. Writers added **checksums** so readers could skip padding and fragments, and unique record IDs so readers could drop duplicates. GFS had pushed part of the correctness burden up to the application. That was acceptable for batch jobs written by a few teams at Google. As more teams and kinds of applications arrived, it became painful.
takeaway: Weak guarantees at the bottom get paid for many times at the top.
deeper:
**Self-validating records:** Each record carries a checksum, so a reader scanning the file recognizes padding and partial garbage as invalid. Each also carries a unique ID, so a reader that meets the same ID twice discards the repeat.

**An organizational cost:** Relaxed consistency kept the file system simpler and fast at concurrent appends. But every consumer now had to know about duplicates and garbage regions. Any team that forgot, or needed strict semantics, got subtle bugs. Relaxed consistency leaking into every application is one of the reasons GFS hit its limits.

**What came after:** Azure's stream layer was designed with strong consistency from the start. Tectonic uses a single writer per file with linearizable metadata. Both keep the guarantee in the storage layer, where it is paid for once instead of in every reader.

quiz.q: A new team reads files produced by GFS record append and treats every record as unique and valid. Which two bugs will they hit?
quiz.a: Duplicate records from retried appends, and padding or partial garbage from failed attempts. They need record IDs to drop duplicates and checksums to skip bad regions.

mcq.q: Why was pushing cleanup onto GFS applications acceptable at first?
options: Users were batch jobs from a few teams
Record append never produced duplicates
The master computed every checksum
Readers always went to the primary
mcq.why: A few teams writing batch jobs could handle duplicates and garbage. As more teams and application types arrived, the burden became painful.

hook: A GFS node vanishes, taking its chunks with it. The system's first move is to do nothing. Why wait?
title: GFS waited 15 minutes before repairing a lost node
body: When a GFS node became unavailable, the system typically waited 15 minutes before re-replicating its chunks. Most unavailability is short. Copying immediately would move huge amounts of data for machines that soon come back. GFS had other patient ideas too: **lazy deletion** through background garbage collection, read-only **shadow masters** when the master was down, and copy-on-write snapshots.

stat.label: GFS wait before re-replicating a lost node

takeaway: Don't repair a failure before you know it's real.
deeper:
**Where the 15 comes from:** Google's 2010 OSDI availability paper reports that GFS typically waited 15 minutes. The delay filters out transient blips, such as a reboot, while still repairing real failures promptly. Disk and network bandwidth stay free for real traffic.

**The other extras:** Lazy deletion lets a batched background process reclaim space, which is simpler than synchronously deleting replicas across many machines and leaves a window to recover from mistakes. Shadow masters give read-only access during a master outage, possibly slightly behind. Copy-on-write snapshots share chunks with the original until one side is modified.

**Scale in 2003:** The largest GFS clusters had over 1,000 storage nodes, over 300 TB of disk, and hundreds of clients. Colossus would later scale over 100× beyond the largest GFS clusters.

quiz.q: A GFS rack drops off the network for 2 minutes during a switch reboot. Why is it good that no re-replication started?
quiz.a: The nodes returned within the 15-minute delay, so GFS avoided copying huge amounts of data for chunks that were never lost, keeping disk and network bandwidth for real traffic.

mcq.q: What do GFS shadow masters do while the master is down?
options: Serve read-only metadata requests
Accept writes until the master returns
Re-replicate chunks from dead nodes
Grant leases to new primaries
mcq.why: Shadow masters give read-only access during a master outage, keeping reads available, though possibly slightly behind.

predict.q: A GFS chunkserver becomes unreachable. How long did GFS typically wait before re-replicating its chunks?
options: About 15 minutes
No wait: it starts immediately
About 24 hours

hook: Petabytes of GFS data needed only a few GB of master RAM. So what actually broke the single master?
title: GFS's real limit was file count, not bytes
body: Take under 64 bytes per 64 MB chunk: 1 PB is about 16 million chunks, so about 1 GB of master RAM. That looks fine. But **file count**, not bytes, is the real limit. A billion small files means a billion namespace entries in one machine's RAM. And one master means one CPU and one NIC for every metadata operation, so thousands of MapReduce tasks opening files at once turn it into a queue.

stat.label: master RAM per PB of chunk metadata

takeaway: Size metadata by file count. Byte math assumes big files and flatters you.
deeper:
**Five limits, in full:**
1. File count: namespace entries grow with files, whatever their size.
2. One CPU and one NIC serve every metadata operation.
3. 64 MB chunks and batch design don't fit latency-sensitive services.
4. Recovery takes time: load the checkpoint, replay the log, and writes stop meanwhile.
5. Relaxed consistency leaked into every application.

**Why the 1 GB misleads:** The chunk figure comes straight from the paper. The danger is the unstated assumption that files are large. Shift the workload toward small files and each one pays a fixed namespace cost, turning a comfortable design into a failing one.

**Three resources:** RAM, CPU and recovery time are the metadata resources, and any of them can run out first. Label the assumptions in your capacity math, especially the ones about file size.

quiz.q: Cluster A holds 1 PB in 10,000 large files. Cluster B holds 100 TB in a billion small files. Each has one GFS-style master. Which master struggles first?
quiz.a: B. Namespace entries grow with file count: a billion entries dwarfs A's 10,000 files plus about 16 million chunks, and B's many opens also queue on one CPU.

mcq.q: Why did thousands of MapReduce tasks starting at once hurt GFS?
options: Their file opens queued on one master's CPU and NIC
Their reads saturated the master's disks
Each task needed its own new 64 MB chunk
They used up the chunkservers' lease slots
mcq.why: Every metadata operation went through one master with one CPU and one network card, so a burst of opens formed a queue.

hook: In 2009, GFS's own tech lead publicly listed what his system could no longer do. What was on the list?
title: GFS's tech lead on why one master wasn't enough
body: A single master had carried Google a long way, until it became the problem. In a 2009 ACM Queue interview, GFS tech lead Sean Quinlan described the pains: file counts growing on a single master, a move to running multiple GFS **cells** and masters, a poor fit for latency-sensitive applications, and work on a new design with distributed masters. Google's 2021 Colossus post confirms the outcome: Colossus was built to fix GFS's metadata scaling limits.
takeaway: Central design, then partition workarounds, then distributed metadata. The arc repeats.
deeper:
**Cells as a stopgap:** Running multiple cells, each with its own master, is static partitioning. It buys headroom but pushes complexity onto users, who must know which cell holds their data. It does nothing for one hot namespace.

**New workloads, old design:** GFS was built for batch jobs, where a master failover or a slow chunk transfer barely mattered. Latency-sensitive applications exposed master recovery time and the batch-oriented chunk design.

**Fixing the root:** The eventual answer was to distribute the masters. Colossus stores metadata in Bigtable behind horizontally scaled curators, so it is no longer limited to one machine's RAM. The same arc, simple central design, then partitioning workarounds, then distributed metadata, repeats with HDFS and at Meta. Know which stage your own system is in.

quiz.q: Your company runs 12 separate clusters because one metadata server can't hold everything. Why is this a stopgap rather than a fix?
quiz.a: It is static partitioning, like Google's multiple GFS cells. Users must track which cluster holds what, and no single namespace can outgrow one server. The fix is distributed metadata.

mcq.q: What did Colossus change to fix GFS's metadata scaling limits?
options: Stored metadata in Bigtable behind curators
Raised the chunk size from 64 MB to 1 GB
Let shadow masters accept writes
Ran many GFS cells under one master
mcq.why: Curators store metadata in Bigtable and scale horizontally, so metadata is no longer limited to one machine's RAM.

hook: The single master that will one day limit your system is not the mistake. So what is?
title: A single master is fine. No exit plan is not.
body: A young system with one metadata master gets simple code and strong metadata semantics. GFS shipped that way and fit Google's early crawl and MapReduce workloads. The trouble arrives later, quietly. Three resources grow with the system: the master's **RAM**, its **CPU**, and its **recovery time** after a crash. One of them runs out first. Teams that never asked which one, and when, find out during an outage instead of a planning meeting.
takeaway: Simplicity is a loan. Know which resource calls it in, and when.
deeper:
**Three different clocks:** RAM grows with file and block count. CPU grows with metadata operations per second, and thousands of MapReduce tasks opening files at once turn one master into a queue. Recovery time grows with the checkpoint plus log to replay, and writes stop while it runs.

**Two escape routes:** HDFS took the incremental path: federation, then high availability, then Observer NameNodes serving reads. Google took the redesign path and built Colossus, which stores metadata in Bigtable behind horizontally scaled curators.

**The review question:** For any centralized metadata design, ask which of the three resources hits its ceiling first, and on what date at current growth. If nobody can answer, an incident will schedule the redesign for you. Knowing the date lets you pick the escape route calmly.

quiz.q: A team says their single metadata master has 70% free RAM, so scaling is years away. Which two checks are they missing?
quiz.a: CPU, because metadata operations per second can queue on one machine during job bursts, and recovery time, because loading the checkpoint and replaying the log stops writes and grows with the namespace.

mcq.q: For a young system with a single metadata master, what is the real mistake?
options: Having no plan for outgrowing the master
Choosing a single master in the first place
Keeping metadata in RAM instead of on disk
Logging changes instead of only checkpointing
mcq.why: A single master gives simple code and strong semantics early. The failure is not knowing which resource, RAM, CPU or recovery time, runs out first.

hook: Google's successor to GFS stores exabytes. Its most complex part doesn't run on a storage server at all.
title: In Colossus, the smartest code lives in the client
body: Google has never published a full Colossus paper. What is public comes from Google Cloud blog posts in 2021 and 2025 and a few research papers. The April 2021 post names five parts: client library, curators, a metadata database in Bigtable, D file servers and custodians. The most complex is the **client library**. It implements **software RAID** and chooses the encoding, replication or erasure codes, to trade performance against cost. Encoding happens before bytes leave the client.
takeaway: If the client does the encoding, the servers can stay simple.
deeper:
**Why push it client-side:** The client already holds the bytes, so it can split and protect them before they touch the network. Storage servers then only store and serve fragments, and applications can pick encodings that suit them.

**The price:** The client library becomes the component that must be correct and carefully upgraded. A bug there affects data layout for every application using it. Tectonic makes the same bet: its client library does replication or Reed-Solomon encoding so each tenant can tune behavior.

**Source discipline:** Colossus is widely discussed and often described with invented detail. Stick to what the 2021 and 2025 posts and related papers say. For example, Google has not published how the metadata stack bottoms out, even though Bigtable itself stores data on a file system. Label anything else as a guess.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes moving erasure-coding logic into Colossus's D file servers to "offload the clients". Which published design choice does that reverse?
quiz.a: Colossus deliberately encodes in the client library, which implements software RAID and chooses replication or erasure codes. D file servers are network-attached disks that just store and serve the fragments.

mcq.q: Which Colossus component chooses between replication and erasure coding?
options: The client library
The curators
The custodians
The D file servers
mcq.why: The client library implements software RAID and picks the encoding. Curators handle control operations, custodians repair and rebalance, D servers store bytes.

hook: Colossus scaled far past the biggest GFS cluster. The trick was changing where file names live.
title: Metadata leaves one machine, and Colossus scales 100×
body: GFS kept all metadata in one master's RAM, so file count hit a hard ceiling. Colossus replaced the master with **curators**, a control plane that scales horizontally. Clients call curators for control operations like creating a file. Curators keep file system metadata in **Bigtable**, a distributed database, not in their own memory. With metadata no longer capped by one machine, Colossus reached exabytes and tens of thousands of machines in one cluster.

stat.label: scale beyond the largest GFS clusters

takeaway: When metadata outgrows one machine, make it rows in a sharded database.
deeper:
**What scales now:** Adding curators adds control-plane capacity, and Bigtable spreads the metadata across many servers. Neither one server's RAM, nor one CPU, nor one recovery log caps the system the way the GFS master did.

**The new weakness:** Metadata in a distributed database makes cross-shard operations hard. A rename that must change rows on several shards atomically is trivial in one process and awkward across partitions. The file system also inherits the database's behavior.

**The recursion:** Bigtable stores its own data on a file system, so the chain must bottom out in something smaller and simpler. Google has not published what that is. Tectonic later made the same move with ZippyDB, and JuiceFS offers it to anyone with Redis or TiKV and an object store.

quiz.q: You move your file system's metadata from one master into a sharded database. Which operation should you expect to get harder, and why?
quiz.a: Cross-shard operations such as rename. They must change rows on several shards atomically, which was trivial inside one master's memory.

mcq.q: What change let Colossus scale over 100× past the largest GFS clusters?
options: Curators store metadata in Bigtable, not one master's RAM
Chunks grew from 64 MB to much larger units
Clients began reading file data through the master
Placement is computed by a hash function, not stored
mcq.why: Bigtable spreads metadata over many servers and curators scale horizontally, so metadata is no longer limited to one machine's RAM.

hook: Colossus curators never touch your bytes, and they don't repair them either. So who does?
title: Colossus splits bytes, control and repair into three jobs
body: A control plane in the data path becomes a bottleneck, and one that also runs repair slows down exactly when disks fail. Colossus separates the jobs. **D file servers** are network-attached disks, and data flows directly between clients and D servers with minimal network hops. **Custodians** are background services that keep data durable and available: they rebalance disk space and run RAID reconstruction, rebuilding lost fragments. Curators handle only control operations like create, open and delete.
takeaway: Keep the control plane out of the data path and the repair path.
deeper:
**Thin disk servers:** The client library has already chosen the encoding and computed the fragments. D servers just store and serve bytes, on HDD or SSD. With nothing between client and disk, a read takes the shortest path.

**What reconstruction means:** With erasure coding, a lost fragment is not copied from a twin. It is recomputed from surviving fragments, which is the RAID reconstruction custodians run. Rebalancing moves data when disks fill unevenly, so capacity and load stay spread.

**Same shape elsewhere:** Tectonic runs background services for garbage collection, repair, rebalancing and rack drains. In GFS, the single master sent chunkservers instructions over heartbeats. Colossus hands this housekeeping to dedicated services, so repair capacity can grow separately from metadata operations.

quiz.q: A disk holding one erasure-coded fragment dies in Colossus. Which component restores durability, and how does that differ from copying a replica?
quiz.a: Custodians run RAID reconstruction: they read surviving fragments and recompute the missing one, instead of copying an identical full replica from another server.

mcq.q: In Colossus, how does file data travel between an application and disk?
options: Directly between the client and D file servers
Through the curators, which forward it to disks
Through custodians, which encode it on the way
Through Bigtable, which stores it next to metadata
mcq.why: Curators handle only control operations. Data flows directly between the client library and D file servers with minimal network hops.

hook: Google never announced Colossus's move off 3× replication. Two public documents give it away anyway.
title: Two public sources reveal Colossus's move to RS codes
body: Google has not published Colossus's encoding mix, yet the shift is traceable. A 2010 Google OSDI paper on availability modeled replication and **Reed-Solomon** encodings in Google's storage cells; the cells it validated against mostly used RS(5,3) and 3× replication. It discussed schemes like RS(6,3) in each of three cells and said its analysis influenced Google's "next generation distributed storage system". The 2021 Colossus post adds client-side software RAID. Together: much data moved from 3× replication to RS, encoded by the client.
takeaway: Connect documented facts, then label the conclusion as an inference.
deeper:
**Why Reed-Solomon:** RS codes split data into data fragments plus parity fragments, and enough surviving fragments rebuild the original. That costs far less space than three full copies. The price is more work to rebuild a lost fragment and more complex writes, one reason a capable client doing the encoding matters.

**The paper's other legacy:** It is also the source for a GFS detail: GFS typically waited 15 minutes before re-replicating chunks from an unavailable node, since most unavailability is short.

**Reading partial disclosures:** Neither document alone says Colossus uses Reed-Solomon for much of its data. One shows the encodings and their influence on the next design. The other shows client-side RAID choosing between replication and erasure codes. That is how to reason about a system that is only partly public: cite what is documented, and mark the conclusion.

quiz.q: A blog post claims "Colossus stores everything in RS(6,3)". Based on what Google has published, what can you actually support?
quiz.a: Only that much data likely moved from 3× replication to Reed-Solomon, encoded client-side. The 2010 paper mentions RS(5,3) and RS(6,3) schemes, but no source gives Colossus's exact mix.

mcq.q: Which pair of sources supports the claim that Colossus moved much data to Reed-Solomon?
options: The 2010 OSDI availability paper and the 2021 Colossus post
The 2003 GFS paper and the 2009 ACM Queue interview
The 2021 Tectonic paper and the 2011 Azure paper
The 2025 Colossus posts and the HDFS erasure-coding docs
mcq.why: The 2010 paper modeled RS encodings and influenced the next-generation system; the 2021 post describes client-side software RAID choosing encodings.

hook: Google runs file systems measured in exabytes on hard disks. So how does hot data still get flash speed?
title: Colossus in 2025: two file systems past 10 EB each
body: In March 2025, Google said many Colossus file systems hold multiple exabytes and two exceed 10 EB each. Reads regularly top 50 TB/s and writes 25 TB/s, and the busiest cluster serves over 600 million IOPS. There is one zonal Colossus file system per cluster, and it is append-only. Hard disks are cheap per byte but short on IOPS, so an SSD cache called **L4** and an ML-based policy decide which data lives on SSD versus HDD.
takeaway: Keep bytes on disk, put heat on flash, and let a policy choose.
deeper:
**Why a cache:** All-SSD would be expensive at multi-exabyte scale. All-HDD would bottleneck on operations per second for hot data. L4 cache index servers answer whether data is cached, a hit or a miss, before the client goes to D file servers. An ML-based policy makes the placement call instead of hand-written tiering rules.

**Why append-only helps:** Written bytes never change, so replication, encoding and caching never chase in-place updates. Azure's stream layer and Tectonic make the same choice.

**What the numbers mean:** A single file system past 10 EB would be unthinkable with a GFS-style master holding every entry in RAM. Moving metadata into Bigtable behind curators is what let Colossus keep growing.

quiz.q: Your team proposes moving a multi-exabyte dataset entirely to SSD for speed. Using Colossus as the model, what is the counter-proposal?
quiz.a: Keep most bytes on cheap HDD and put only hot data on an SSD cache, the way Colossus uses L4 with an ML-based policy to choose what lives on flash.

mcq.q: What decides whether Colossus data lives on SSD or HDD?
options: An SSD cache called L4 with an ML-based policy
Curators, based on each file's creation date
A fixed rule that places all appends on SSD
The application, through a per-file storage class
mcq.why: Google's March 2025 post says the L4 SSD cache and an ML-based policy choose which data lives on SSD versus HDD.

predict.q: How much data do the largest Colossus file systems hold (2025)?
options: Over 10 EB each
About 300 PB each
About 1 EB each

hook: Colossus sits on disks, yet acknowledges durable appends in under a millisecond. What does it skip?
title: How Colossus makes durable appends sub-millisecond
body: Looking up locations on every request adds a round trip before any byte moves. Colossus's **stateful protocol**, described in April 2025, pays that cost once. On open, the client gets a handle holding the data's disk locations, then talks to disks directly over an RDMA-like protocol. A durable append writes to several disks in parallel and completes once a **quorum** has it. Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery use it, and it powers Cloud Storage Rapid Storage.
takeaway: Look up once, write in parallel, and never wait for the slowest disk.
deeper:
**What stateful means:** The client keeps the location information it got at open, so later operations skip metadata lookups and go straight to disks. The RDMA-like protocol keeps software overhead on that path small, which matters at sub-millisecond targets.

**Why a quorum:** Waiting for every disk means waiting for the slowest one. Acknowledging once a quorum has the data keeps one slow disk off the critical path. Tectonic's blob storage uses the same quorum-append idea and adds hedged writes.

**How far from GFS:** GFS was built for sustained bandwidth over latency, and its poor fit for latency-sensitive services was one of its documented pains. The same lineage now backs Google's databases and Rapid Storage, which handles up to 20 million requests per second in one bucket.

quiz.q: One disk in a Colossus append group is having a slow day. Why doesn't every append now take as long as that disk?
quiz.a: Appends go to several disks in parallel and are acknowledged once a quorum has the data, so the slow disk is not on the critical path.

mcq.q: What does a Colossus client receive when it opens a file under the stateful protocol?
options: A handle containing the data's disk locations
A lease making it the primary for each chunk
A copy of the file's metadata rows from Bigtable
A token that routes each request through curators
mcq.why: The handle carries disk locations, so the client talks to disks directly over an RDMA-like protocol without further lookups.

hook: Colossus keeps its metadata in Bigtable. Bigtable keeps its data on a file system. Where does it end?
title: A file system whose metadata leans on a file system
body: Colossus keeps file system metadata in Bigtable, a scalable database. But that database stores its own data on a file system, so the design is recursive. Tectonic repeats the metadata-in-a-database pattern with ZippyDB. Recursion is survivable because each level is far smaller than the one above: metadata is a sliver of the data, and the metadata's own storage is a sliver of that. Still, the chain must bottom out in something smaller and simpler. Google has not published what it is.
takeaway: Every recursive stack needs a base that can start cold on its own.
deeper:
**The cold-start risk:** If the database needs the file system to start, and the file system needs the database to serve metadata, a full outage could deadlock. The base layer has to come up without either. That is why it must be smaller, simpler and self-sufficient.

**What is public:** Curators store metadata in Bigtable. How the recursion ends is unpublished. Online claims that describe the base layer in detail are guesses, so treat them that way in a design review.

**Who else does it:** Tectonic stores its Name, File and Block layers in ZippyDB, Meta's sharded key-value store. JuiceFS packages the idea for anyone: metadata in an engine like Redis or TiKV, data in an object store. For any of them, ask one question: what sits at the bottom, and how does it restart from zero?

quiz.q: Every server in a Colossus-style cluster reboots at once. Why can't the file system and its metadata database simply wait for each other?
quiz.a: Each depends on the other: the database stores data on a file system, and the file system keeps metadata in the database. A smaller, independent base layer must start first.

mcq.q: What has Google published about how the Colossus and Bigtable recursion bottoms out?
options: Nothing; those details are unpublished
It ends in the original GFS master
It ends in a small ZippyDB cluster on SSD
It ends in a Paxos-replicated stream manager
mcq.why: Google's posts describe metadata in Bigtable but not the base of the stack, so specific claims about it are speculation.

hook: Yahoo, Facebook, LinkedIn and Uber all ran a near piece-for-piece copy of one Google system.
title: HDFS is GFS with new names
body: The **Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS)** began as open source modeled on GFS, and it powered the Hadoop era at thousands of companies. The mapping is almost one-to-one. The **NameNode** is the master: one metadata server holding the full namespace and block map in RAM. DataNodes are the chunkservers, storing blocks of typically 128 MB. The NameNode persists the namespace in an FsImage and logs every change to the EditLog, like GFS's checkpoint and operation log.
takeaway: Copy an architecture and you copy its ceiling too.
deeper:
**Restart path:** The FsImage is a snapshot of the namespace, and the EditLog records every change since. On restart the NameNode loads the FsImage and replays the EditLog, the same recovery shape GFS used.

**Who knows where blocks are:** DataNodes send heartbeats and block reports, the list of blocks they hold, to the NameNode. As in GFS, the storage nodes are the source of truth for locations.

**What files can do:** HDFS is write-once-read-many: files are written once, with support for append and truncate. That fits batch analytics.

**The inherited limit:** All metadata sits in one process's memory, and every metadata operation goes through one server. Federation, high availability and Observer NameNodes are all later attempts to push that single-master ceiling.

quiz.q: A colleague who knows GFS asks what an HDFS block report is. How do you explain it in GFS terms?
quiz.a: It is how GFS chunkservers told the master which chunks they held: each DataNode lists its blocks, so the NameNode learns locations from DataNodes rather than storing them as truth.

mcq.q: Which HDFS component corresponds to the GFS master?
options: The NameNode
The DataNode
The JournalNode
The EditLog
mcq.why: The NameNode is the single metadata server holding the namespace and block map in RAM, as the GFS master did. DataNodes map to chunkservers.

hook: HDFS survives losing a whole rack, yet puts two of its three copies in the same rack. Why?
title: Three replicas, two racks, one cross-rack hop
body: Put all three replicas in one rack and a rack failure takes them all. Put them in three racks and every write crosses racks twice. HDFS's **rack-aware placement** splits the difference: the first replica goes on the writer's node or a random node in its rack, the second on a node in a different rack, the third on another node in that same remote rack. A rack loss still leaves a copy, and each write crosses racks once.
takeaway: Survive the failure domain once; don't pay to cross it twice.
deeper:
**Why the hop count matters:** HDFS writes follow a pipeline like GFS's chain: the client sends data to the first DataNode, which forwards to the second, which forwards to the third. With this layout only the first-to-second hop leaves a rack. The second-to-third hop stays inside the remote rack.

**Why the writer's node first:** The first copy lands next to the writer, so that hop stays local too. The whole write pays for exactly one trip across racks.

**The same idea as a rule:** This is failure-domain thinking turned into a fixed policy. Ceph expresses it as a CRUSH rule, such as "3 replicas in 3 different racks", computed by a function any client can run instead of decided by a central server.

quiz.q: A team changes HDFS placement to put the three replicas in three different racks "for safety". What do they pay, and what do they gain?
quiz.a: Every write now crosses racks twice instead of once, using more cross-rack bandwidth. They gain survival of two simultaneous rack failures; the default already survives one.

mcq.q: Where does HDFS put the third replica by default?
options: On a different node in the second replica's rack
On a third rack chosen at random
On the writer's own node
On the node with the most free space
mcq.why: The third replica shares the remote rack with the second, so the block survives a rack loss while each write crosses racks only once.

predict.q: HDFS keeps 3 replicas and survives a full rack failure. How many racks does it use per block?
options: Two
Three
One

hook: An HDFS file can be any size, but every one takes a slice of one server's RAM. How big a slice?
title: An average HDFS file costs about 600 bytes of NameNode RAM
body: Konstantin Shvachko, then at Yahoo, did the NameNode math in 2010. Each **metadata object**, a file or a block, costs under 200 bytes. An average file had 1.5 blocks, so about 600 bytes: one file object plus two block objects. At that rate, 100 million files need at least 60 GB of NameNode RAM. His rule of thumb: 1 GB of metadata per 1 PB of physical storage.

stat.label: NameNode RAM per average HDFS file

takeaway: In HDFS you run out of names before you run out of disk.
deeper:
**Scale it up:** 500 million average files need about 600 bytes × 500 million, roughly 300 GB of RAM. That lands in the same range as LinkedIn's later 380 GB NameNode heap holding about 1 billion objects.

**Why two blocks, not 1.5:** The estimate rounds up to 3 objects × 200 bytes, so it errs on the generous side.

**Where the rule breaks:** 1 GB per PB assumes typical file sizes. Tiny files blow it up, because each file pays the object cost whatever its size. That makes small files a NameNode capacity problem, not a tuning problem.

**Failure is routine:** Shvachko also reported 2 to 3 node failures per 1,000 nodes per day on Yahoo's long-running clusters. On a 4,000-node cluster that is roughly 8 to 12 failures every day.

quiz.q: Two HDFS clusters each store 1 PB. One holds 1 GB files, the other 1 MB files. Which needs more NameNode RAM, and roughly how much more?
quiz.a: The 1 MB cluster: about a billion files versus a million. Counting all objects (about 2 per 1 MB file, 9 per 1 GB file with 128 MB blocks), it needs roughly 200× more RAM.

mcq.q: Why does an average HDFS file cost about 600 bytes of NameNode RAM?
options: One file object plus two block objects, each under 200 bytes
One 600-byte inode stored for each replica of the file
Three replicas, each tracked with its own 200-byte record
A fixed 600-byte header attached to every block
mcq.why: Shvachko counted under 200 bytes per metadata object. An average 1.5-block file rounds up to one file object and two block objects.

hook: An HDFS NameNode can have plenty of RAM left and still stall a whole cluster. What is choking it?
title: Uber's NameNode: 10 ms queues became 500 ms at peak
body: RAM is the NameNode's first limit. The second is **RPC throughput**: every open, list and block report is a remote call to one Java process. On a huge heap, **garbage collection** pauses make it worse, because calls pile up while the JVM reclaims memory. Uber hit this in late 2016, with NameNode RPC queue times of 500 ms at peak against a normal 10 ms. Every client waiting on an open or list waited in that queue.
takeaway: A bigger heap buys namespace and sells latency.
deeper:
**The feedback loop:** It compounds.
1. A bigger namespace needs a bigger heap.
2. A bigger heap brings longer or more frequent GC pauses.
3. Pauses raise latency for every caller, including DataNodes sending block reports.

**Hidden load:** DataNodes are the source of truth for block locations, so thousands of them send lists of every block they hold, and one process must digest them all.

**What helped:** Uber tuned GC on its 160 GB NameNode heap, cutting GC pause time from 13% to 1.7%. It also split the namespace behind ViewFs and adopted the Observer NameNode to offload reads. LinkedIn later found that switching the NameNode lock to non-fair mode gave about 10× better performance, more evidence that the bottleneck was contention inside one process.

quiz.q: An ops team doubles the NameNode heap to fit more files, and metadata latency gets worse. What happened?
quiz.a: The larger Java heap brought longer or more frequent GC pauses. During a pause every RPC queues, so latency rises for all clients, including DataNodes sending block reports.

mcq.q: Besides RAM, what is the HDFS NameNode's second scaling limit?
options: RPC throughput through one Java process
Disk bandwidth on the DataNodes
Cross-rack bandwidth during writes
The number of JournalNodes in the quorum
mcq.why: Every open, list and block report is an RPC to one Java process, and GC pauses on a huge heap make the queue worse.

predict.q: Uber's normal NameNode RPC queue time was 10 ms. What did it reach at peak in late 2016?
options: 500 ms
20 ms
5 seconds

hook: HDFS added NameNodes to share the load, yet one busy directory can still swamp a single server. Why?
title: Federation adds NameNodes, but hot directories stay hot
body: One NameNode can't hold everything, so Hadoop 2 added **Federation**: several independent NameNodes, each owning a separate namespace with its own block pool. DataNodes store blocks for all pools and report to every NameNode, so disks stay shared. Clients see one tree through ViewFs mount tables or Router-based Federation. The catch is **static partitioning**. Someone decides which directory lives on which NameNode, and a hot directory stays on one server.
takeaway: Static partitioning moves the bottleneck around; it never dissolves it.
deeper:
**The mount-table analogy:** ViewFs works like mounting several file systems into one Unix directory tree. Paths under one prefix go to one NameNode, paths under another go elsewhere. Router-based Federation moves that mapping into routers so every client need not carry it.

**What you gain:** Total metadata RAM, CPU and RPC capacity grow with the number of NameNodes, while DataNodes stay one shared pool.

**What you still pay:** Balancing is manual: someone must notice an overloaded NameNode and move directories. Moving files between namespaces is a copy, not a rename, because different NameNodes own the trees. One very busy directory cannot be split at all.

**Who used it:** Uber split HDFS into namespaces behind ViewFs. Federation is an easy step from one master, but it postpones metadata scaling rather than solving it.

quiz.q: A federated HDFS cluster must move /logs from NameNode A's namespace to NameNode B's. Why is this far slower than a rename inside one namespace?
quiz.a: Each NameNode owns a separate tree, so a cross-namespace move is a copy of the data, not a metadata update.

mcq.q: What is the main weakness of HDFS Federation?
options: Directories are assigned statically, so hot ones stay hot
DataNodes can store blocks for only one namespace
Clients must contact every NameNode for each read
Each NameNode needs its own separate set of disks
mcq.why: Operators decide which directory lives on which NameNode. Balancing is manual, and a busy directory stays on one server.

hook: Two HDFS NameNodes both believe they're in charge and accept conflicting writes. What stops that?
title: HDFS HA: one writer, a majority of JournalNodes
body: One NameNode is a single point of failure, but two active ones would corrupt the namespace with conflicting edits, a **split brain**. HDFS high availability uses the **Quorum Journal Manager**. The active NameNode writes each edit to a majority of an odd number, at least 3, of JournalNodes. Only one NameNode may write to them, and fencing stops an old active. Standbys tail the edits and must read all of them before taking over.
takeaway: High availability buys you a spare, not more capacity.
deeper:
**Why a majority:** With 3 JournalNodes an edit is safe once 2 have it, so one can fail without losing edits or blocking writes. With 5, two can fail.

**Why read everything first:** A standby must apply all edits before becoming active. Otherwise it could come up missing changes already acknowledged to clients.

**Who pulls the trigger:** A ZKFailoverController (ZKFC) runs beside each NameNode, health-checks it, and uses ZooKeeper for leader election and automatic failover. Nobody has to be paged to flip it.

**What HA does not do:** There is still one active NameNode taking all writes, and until Observer NameNodes arrived, all reads too. HA fixes availability. It adds no metadata capacity at all. Capacity comes from federation and Observer NameNodes.

quiz.q: An old active NameNode was only cut off, not dead, and comes back still thinking it leads. Why can't it corrupt the namespace?
quiz.a: Only one NameNode may write to the JournalNodes, so it cannot commit edits once a new active holds that right, and fencing stops it from continuing as active.

mcq.q: With 5 JournalNodes, how many can fail while HDFS keeps accepting edits?
mcq.why: Each edit needs a majority. With 5 JournalNodes, 3 must have it, so up to 2 can fail.

hook: You create a file on HDFS, then list its directory through a read replica. How do you avoid seeing nothing?
title: How HDFS read replicas keep your own writes visible
body: Most NameNode traffic is reads, so the **Observer NameNode** tails the edit log and serves reads while the active serves writes. The hard part is **read-your-writes**: a follower may lag, yet a client that just created a file must see it. So the client tracks the latest transaction ID it has seen, its **state ID**. An observer that hasn't caught up to that ID waits before answering. For consistency across clients, `msync()` fetches the active's current state ID.
takeaway: A replica may lag. It just can't answer until it catches up to you.
deeper:
**The protocol:** Three steps.
1. The client writes on the active and learns the new transaction ID.
2. Its next read to an observer carries the highest ID it has seen.
3. If the observer hasn't applied that edit yet, it holds the request until it has.

**Across clients:** If client A writes and tells client B out of band, B has never seen A's ID. B calls `msync()` to fetch the active's current state ID, then reads from an observer safely.

**The payoff:** At LinkedIn, observers handle reads, about 95% of operations. RPC latency dropped to 1 to 2 ms from under 10 ms, and namespace throughput rose about 3×. Uber adopted observers too. The limit remains: every write still lands on one node.

quiz.q: Service A writes a file to HDFS, then messages service B, which immediately reads through an observer and sees nothing. What should B have done?
quiz.a: Called msync() to fetch the active NameNode's current state ID, so the observer waits until it has applied edits up to that point before answering.

mcq.q: What does an Observer NameNode do when a client's state ID is ahead of its own?
options: Waits until it has applied edits up to that ID
Forwards the read to the active NameNode
Returns its current view and flags it as stale
Resets the client's state ID to its own
mcq.why: The client sends the latest state ID it has seen; the observer holds the request until it catches up, so the client never sees older state.

hook: HDFS found a way to cut its extra storage from 200% to 50%. Why doesn't everyone use it for all data?
title: Hadoop 3 erasure coding: 50% extra instead of 200%
body: Three full replicas store 200% extra. Hadoop 3 added striped **erasure coding**: a file is split into small cells, 1 MB in the built-in policies, striped across a group of DataNodes. The default policy, RS-6-3-1024k, adds 3 parity cells per 6 data cells, so 6 blocks' worth of data takes 9 blocks of space instead of 18. The savings come with strings attached: hardware layout rules and missing file operations.

stat.label: extra storage with RS-6-3, versus 200% for 3×

takeaway: Erasure coding is for data that has finished changing.
deeper:
**Layout rules:** RS(6,3) needs at least 9 DataNodes and 3 racks, ideally 9 racks, to spread a stripe across failure domains. Most EC traffic crosses racks, so network bisection bandwidth, the capacity between halves of the network, becomes critical.

**Missing operations:** `append()`, `truncate()`, `concat()` and `hflush()` do not work on EC files. Parity covers a whole stripe, so growing one or flushing part of it is awkward. That confines EC to warm and cold data.

**Same trade, other systems:** Azure replicates active extents and erasure codes them only after sealing. Tectonic's blob path replicates first and re-encodes to RS(10,4) later, while its warehouse writes RS(9,6) directly because files are written whole. HDFS stripes per file, which suits data that is already complete and rarely touched again.

quiz.q: A team wants to erasure code a directory of hot log files that producers append to all day. What breaks?
quiz.a: append() and hflush() don't work on HDFS EC files, so producers can't keep appending or flushing. Keep hot, appended data replicated and erasure code it once it goes cold.

mcq.q: Why does Hadoop 3's RS-6-3 policy suit warm and cold data best?
options: EC files don't support append, truncate, concat or hflush
EC files can only be read from inside a single rack
EC doubles storage overhead compared with replication
EC needs fewer DataNodes than replication does
mcq.why: append(), truncate(), concat() and hflush() fail on EC files, so EC fits data that has stopped changing.

hook: Uber's HDFS data grew 400% in one year. No single fix could keep up. What did?
title: Uber's 400% HDFS year took six fixes
body: Uber's HDFS data grew 400% in 2017 alone, and its NameNode RPC queues had already hit 500 ms at peak in late 2016. So Uber, reporting in 2018, attacked from every side. It split HDFS into namespaces behind ViewFs, upgraded HDFS, tuned garbage collection on a 160 GB NameNode heap, built a **stitcher** to merge small files, set **quotas**, and adopted the Observer NameNode. GC pause time fell from 13% to 1.7%.
takeaway: When one server is the ceiling, every fix is a way to ask it less.
deeper:
**Map fixes to limits:** Namespaces behind ViewFs are federation, so each NameNode carries less. GC tuning shortens pauses that stall every RPC. The stitcher merges small files, and because each file costs roughly the same NameNode memory whatever its size, merging frees namespace directly. Quotas cap growth at the source. Observers take read RPCs off the active.

**The Yahoo baseline:** In 2010 Yahoo's biggest clusters had 4,000 nodes and 14 PB, with one namespace holding over 100 million objects. Mind the units: objects are files plus blocks, so that differs from Shvachko's 60 GB estimate for 100 million files, which is about 300 million objects.

**The pattern:** A decade of HDFS operators hit the same single-master limits GFS hit, and reached for the same families of fixes.

quiz.q: Your NameNode heap is nearly full although the disks are half empty, and most files are under 1 MB. Which of Uber's fixes helps most, and why?
quiz.a: The small-file stitcher. Each file costs about the same NameNode memory regardless of size, so merging many small files into fewer large ones frees namespace capacity directly.

mcq.q: What did GC tuning on Uber's 160 GB NameNode heap achieve?
options: GC pause time fell from 13% to 1.7%
RPC queue time fell from 500 ms to 1 ms
Heap use fell from 160 GB to 60 GB
Namespace throughput rose about 10×
mcq.why: Uber reported GC pause time dropping from 13% to 1.7%, easing the RPC queuing that pauses cause on a huge heap.

hook: LinkedIn keeps 500 PB in one Hadoop cluster that still has a single active metadata server. How?
title: LinkedIn: 1 billion objects on one NameNode
body: In "The Exabyte Club" (2021), LinkedIn reported 1 exabyte across its Hadoop clusters. The largest had 10,000 nodes and 500 PB, with about 1 billion objects on a single NameNode using a 380 GB heap. From 2015 to 2020 it grew from 20 PB to 500 PB and from 145 million to 1.6 billion namespace objects, with peak load of 250K operations per second. One writer can go a long way with enough engineering.
takeaway: Find the scarce resource, then shield it from everything that doesn't need it.
deeper:
**Offload the reads:** Observer NameNodes handle reads, about 95% of operations. RPC latency fell to 1 to 2 ms from under 10 ms, and namespace throughput rose about 3×.

**Quarantine small files:** A separate Satellite cluster of just 32 DataNodes holds about 100 million small files. The bytes are few but the file count is huge, so isolating them protects the main NameNode's memory and RPC capacity.

**Fix the lock:** Switching the NameNode lock to non-fair mode gave about 10× better performance. A fair lock hands access strictly in arrival order, which adds overhead under heavy contention.

**Other exits:** Twitter (now X) described a hybrid plan in 2019 to move part of its Hadoop workloads to Google Cloud. Meta replaced all of its HDFS clusters with Tectonic.

quiz.q: Why would LinkedIn stand up a whole cluster, just 32 DataNodes, for about 100 million small files?
quiz.a: Those files cost NameNode memory and RPCs far out of proportion to their bytes. Isolating them protected the main namespace, the resource that actually ran out.

mcq.q: What share of LinkedIn's NameNode operations are reads, served by observers?
options: About 95%
About 50%
About 70%
About 30%
mcq.why: LinkedIn reported reads at about 95% of operations, so moving them to Observer NameNodes cut RPC latency to 1 to 2 ms.

predict.q: LinkedIn's largest Hadoop cluster (2021) ran one active NameNode. How many namespace objects did it hold?
options: About 1 billion
About 100 million
About 10 billion

hook: Your HDFS cluster has petabytes of free disk and still can't take new files. What ran out?
title: Small files fill HDFS's brain, not its disks
body:
