Teams see millions of tiny files slowing HDFS and reach for tuning knobs. Wrong problem. The NameNode holds every file and every block as an object in RAM, fewer than 200 bytes each, whatever the size. A 1 KB file and a 100 MB file each cost one file object plus one block object.

So small files are a **capacity** problem: the namespace fills while the disks sit mostly empty. LinkedIn and Uber both hit the namespace ceiling first.
takeaway: Disks fill by bytes. NameNodes fill by count.
deeper:
**Why tuning fails:** Buffer sizes, caching and job parallelism change how fast you touch metadata, not how much of it exists. The heap keeps filling with file objects either way.

**What actually works:** Change the object count, or where objects live.
1. Merge files: Uber built a stitcher to combine small files.
2. Cap creation: Uber set quotas.
3. Isolate them: LinkedIn keeps about 100 million small files on a separate Satellite cluster of just 32 DataNodes.

**The math of a billion:** A billion 1 KB files hold about 1 TB of data but need a billion file objects and a billion block objects, up to about 400 GB of NameNode heap. LinkedIn's biggest NameNode runs a 380 GB heap for about 1 billion objects. A cluster can be full while its disks are nearly empty.

quiz.q: Two HDFS clusters store 1 PB each. One holds 8 million 128 MB files, the other 1 billion 1 MB files. Which NameNode is in trouble, and why?
quiz.a: The second. NameNode memory scales with object count, not bytes: about 2 billion objects (a file plus a block each) versus about 16 million.

mcq.q: Your HDFS cluster refuses new files while DataNode disks are only 40% full. What is the most likely cause?
options: The NameNode heap is full of small-file metadata
DataNode block reports are arriving too slowly
The replication factor is set too high
Rack-aware placement has run out of racks
mcq.why: Each file costs roughly the same NameNode metadata whatever its size, so many small files exhaust the namespace long before the disks fill.

predict.q: An HDFS cluster fills up with millions of 1 KB files. What runs out first?
options: NameNode memory
DataNode disk space
Network bandwidth

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: Meta's hot-photo store was designed for 3.6 copies of every byte. It ended up paying for far more. Why?
title: Haystack paid 5.3× for a 3.6× design
body: Meta ran hot blobs on Haystack (3× replication plus RAID-6, ideally 3.6×), warm blobs on f4 (RS(10,4) in two datacenters, about 2.8×), and its warehouse on many HDFS clusters. Haystack was IOPS-bound: it bought disks for their speed and left their space idle. f4 had the opposite problem, spare IOPS but no capacity. Each system **stranded** what the other needed.
takeaway: Separate systems waste separately: idle IOPS here, idle terabytes there.
deeper:
**Workload drift:** More blobs were short-lived and got deleted before they ever moved to f4. So more data spent its whole life at Haystack's expensive factor, pushing the effective number up further.

**The warehouse too:** Meta's data warehouse ran on many HDFS clusters, each with its own single NameNode, its own metadata ceiling, and its own spare resources nobody else could touch.

**The fix:** Put blob storage and the warehouse on the same disks, in one multi-tenant file system. On shared disks, one tenant's spare IOPS cover the other's needs instead of sitting idle.

**The prerequisite:** That pool has to hold exabytes in a single datacenter. That needs metadata that scales far past any single NameNode, and that one requirement shaped everything Tectonic became.

quiz.q: Haystack has idle disk space and f4 has idle disk IOPS. Why can't Meta simply shift load between them?
quiz.a: They are separate systems on separate disks, so the spare resources are stranded. Only a shared file system on the same disks lets one tenant's spare IOPS cover another's needs.

mcq.q: Why did Haystack's effective replication climb from an ideal 3.6× to 5.3×?
options: It was IOPS-bound, so it bought disks it could not fill
RAID-6 rebuilds created extra temporary copies
f4 pushed warm blobs back into Haystack
Its erasure code was switched to RS(10,4)
mcq.why: Haystack needed disks for their IOPS, not their space, leaving capacity idle. Short-lived blobs deleted before reaching f4 made it worse.

predict.q: Haystack, Meta's hot-blob store, was designed for 3.6× effective replication. What did it actually reach?
options: 3.6×, as designed

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: Ceph ripped out its local file system after a decade. Meta's exabyte-scale Tectonic kept XFS. Who was wrong?
title: Tectonic stores exabytes as plain XFS files
body:
Tectonic, Meta's file system, can span an entire datacenter and store exabytes. Yet at the bottom, each storage node keeps chunks as ordinary files on local XFS, plus a 1 TB SSD for XFS metadata and hot chunks.

Upper layers see a **block** as a plain array of bytes. Underneath, that block is really a set of replicated or Reed-Solomon encoded chunks spread across storage nodes. Readers never need to know which.
takeaway: Choose your disk layer by write pattern, not by fashion.
deeper:
**Nobody was wrong:** Ceph needs fine-grained updates and transactions, which local file systems handled poorly, so it moved to BlueStore on raw devices. Tectonic mostly writes large immutable chunks, which local file systems handle well.

**Why the SSD:** Hard disks are slow at the small random reads that file system metadata needs. Putting XFS metadata on a 1 TB SSD keeps local lookups fast, and hot chunks get the same boost.

**Three big parts:** The Chunk Store holds data. The Metadata Store maps names to files, files to blocks, and blocks to disks. The Client Library drives both and picks the encoding, while background services run garbage collection, repair and rebalancing.

**Why datacenter scale:** One pool big enough for blob storage and the warehouse together lets their spare resources cover each other on the same disks.

quiz.q: Your new storage system mostly writes large immutable chunks. A colleague cites Ceph's move to BlueStore as proof you must avoid local file systems. Your reply?
quiz.a: Ceph left file systems because it needed fine-grained updates and transactions. Large immutable chunks are exactly what local file systems handle well, which is why Tectonic keeps chunks on XFS.

mcq.q: In Tectonic, what is a block underneath the byte-array view that upper layers see?
options: A set of replicated or RS-encoded chunks on storage nodes
A single 128 MB file on one storage node
A row in ZippyDB holding the raw bytes
A 1 GB extent on a Paxos-replicated node
mcq.why: The Chunk Store protects each block as replicated or Reed-Solomon encoded chunks across nodes. Callers only ever see bytes.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: A disk dies. Which of 15 billion blocks just lost a copy? Tectonic answers without scanning anything.
title: Tectonic splits metadata three ways: Name, File, Block
body: One metadata server can't hold billions of files, so Tectonic breaks metadata apart by kind. The Name layer maps a directory to its children. The File layer maps a file to its blocks. The Block layer maps a block to disk locations, plus a **reverse index** for repair. Each layer lives in **ZippyDB**, Meta's linearizable, sharded key-value store on RocksDB and SSD, and each is hash-partitioned.
takeaway: Split metadata by the question it answers, and each question scales alone.
deeper:
**The repair answer:** The reverse index answers 'which blocks lived on this failed disk?' directly. Without it, finding a dead disk's blocks means scanning every block's location list.

**Different traffic, different layers:** Listing a directory hits the Name layer. Opening and reading a file hits the File and Block layers. Repair and rebalancing hit the Block layer. Separate layers let each be scaled and cached for its own pattern.

**Strong metadata:** ZippyDB is linearizable, so metadata operations appear to happen in one order. That matches Tectonic's model: a single writer per file, with linearizable metadata.

**The catch:** More moving parts and more RPC hops. Opening one file can touch several layers, each a network call. Azure makes a similar split between its stream and partition layers, and ADLS layers metadata too but range-partitions it.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes merging Tectonic's three metadata layers into one table to save RPC hops. What do you give up?
quiz.a: Independent scaling and caching per access pattern. Directory listings, file opens and repair lookups would all contend in one structure instead of each layer growing on its own.

mcq.q: What is the Block layer's reverse index in Tectonic for?
options: Finding which blocks lived on a failed disk
Listing the children of a directory quickly
Ordering writes from several clients to a file
Choosing between replication and RS encoding
mcq.why: Repair needs to know which blocks a dead disk held. The reverse index maps disks to blocks, so no full scan is needed.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: Keeping a directory's entries together makes listing it fast. Tectonic scattered them on purpose. Why?
title: Tectonic hashes metadata so no directory runs hot
body:
Sharded metadata must decide which entries share a shard. **Range partitioning** keeps related keys together, so one directory's entries sit on one shard, and listing it is a single fast scan. Azure Data Lake Store (ADLS) layers its metadata this way.

The cost: a busy directory becomes a hot spot, because all its traffic lands on one shard. Tectonic uses **hash partitioning** instead. Load spreads evenly, at the price of harder multi-item operations.
takeaway: Locality makes scans cheap and hot spots inevitable. Choose which pain you can afford.
deeper:
**How range fails:** Keys are sorted and each shard owns a contiguous range. If thousands of jobs create files in one directory, one shard takes all of it. Adding shards does nothing unless that range can be split.

**How hashing helps:** Each key hashes to a shard, so neighbouring keys scatter. A busy directory's load spreads across many shards instead of pinning one.

**The bill:** Operations that touch many entries, like listing a huge directory or a rename spanning many items, now cross many shards and need coordination. Cross-shard operations such as rename are the known weak spot of metadata kept in a sharded database.

**The general question:** Do your hottest operations need locality, or does even load matter more? Tectonic, serving many tenants from one file system, bet on even load.

quiz.q: A thousand jobs write output files into the same directory at once. Compare range- and hash-partitioned metadata.
quiz.a: Range: every create hits the single shard owning that directory, a hot spot. Hash: creates scatter across many shards, but listing that directory now has to touch many shards.

mcq.q: Why did Tectonic hash-partition its metadata instead of range-partitioning it like ADLS?
options: Hashing spreads a busy directory's load across shards
Hashing turns directory listings into a single scan
Hashing makes cross-directory renames cheaper
Hashing lets ZippyDB skip linearizability
mcq.why: Range partitioning puts a busy directory on one shard, creating a hot spot. Hashing spreads load evenly but makes multi-item operations harder.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: Spread blocks across random disk combinations and almost any few-disk failure destroys some block. Bad idea?
title: Copysets trade how often you lose data for rebuild speed
body:
Tectonic is **client-driven**: the Client Library orchestrates metadata and storage calls and does replication or Reed-Solomon encoding itself, so each tenant tunes its own behaviour. Background services handle garbage collection, repair, rebalancing and rack drains.

They also manage **copysets**, the distinct combinations of disks holding a block. Few combinations make losses rarer, but a rebuild reads from fewer disks. Many combinations spread rebuild load but raise the odds of loss.
takeaway: Placement sets two dials at once: how often you lose data, how fast you heal.
deeper:
**Random placement:** If blocks land on random disk combinations, nearly every set of a few disks holds some block. Any simultaneous failure of that many disks destroys something, though only a little.

**Fixed placement:** If blocks use only a few fixed combinations, most multi-disk failures hit no complete copyset. Losses become rare, but larger when they happen. Rebuilding a failed disk also draws from fewer peers, so reconstruction is slower.

**Managing the middle:** Tectonic's background services manage copysets to balance loss risk against reconstruction load, picking a point between those extremes.

**No central proxy:** Client-driven means data never flows through a middle tier. The client asks the Metadata Store where blocks go, then writes chunks straight to storage nodes. Colossus has the same shape, with a client library doing software RAID.

quiz.q: Your cluster stores every block's three replicas on a random trio of disks. Three disks die at once. What probably happened, and what is the upside of this layout?
quiz.a: Some block very likely lost all three copies, though little data overall. The upside: rebuilding a failed disk reads from many peers in parallel, so reconstruction is fast.

mcq.q: What do Tectonic's background services balance by managing copysets?
options: Data-loss risk against reconstruction load
Read latency against write latency
Metadata size against block size
Tenant isolation against encoding cost
mcq.why: Copysets are the disk combinations holding blocks. Fewer combinations make loss rarer; more spread rebuild work. Tectonic balances the two.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: Meta's warehouse never writes a single replica, not even briefly. So how does it protect its data?
title: Meta's warehouse encodes in RAM and skips replication
body: Tectonic lets each tenant write its own way. The data warehouse writes large files once and reads them only when complete. Nobody reads a half-written block, so the client can buffer a full block, Reed-Solomon encode it in memory, and write each chunk directly. Long-lived data typically uses RS(9,6) across 15 disks; short-lived shuffle files use RS(3,3). Space, disk I/O and network all drop versus replication.
takeaway: If nobody reads it until it's finished, encode it before it's written.
deeper:
**Why it works:** Waiting costs nothing when no reader is waiting. The client gathers a whole block, computes parity once, and writes each chunk exactly once. No replicated copy is ever written, so there is no re-encoding step later.

**Two codes, two lifetimes:** RS(9,6) stores 15 chunks for 9 of data, about 1.67×, and survives the loss of any 6. That suits data kept for a long time. RS(3,3) needs only 6 chunks at 2×, a fit for MapReduce shuffle files that live only as long as a job. Even 2× beats 3× replication.

**The enabler:** Encoding lives in the client library. A server-side system with one global policy could not give the warehouse bulk-encoded writes and blob storage low-latency appends at the same time. Per-tenant clients are the escape hatch that makes one shared file system practical.

quiz.q: Why can't Tectonic's blob storage copy the warehouse trick of buffering a full block and encoding it in memory?
quiz.a: Blob writes are small and need low latency. Waiting to fill a whole block before acknowledging would make every small write slow, so blobs replicate first and encode after sealing.

mcq.q: Which Tectonic data typically uses RS(3,3) rather than RS(9,6)?
options: Short-lived MapReduce shuffle files
Long-lived warehouse data
Hot blob uploads before sealing
XFS metadata on the node's SSD
mcq.why: Shuffle files live only for a job, so a smaller 6-chunk code fits. Long-lived warehouse data uses RS(9,6) across 15 disks.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: Erasure coding one tiny blob means touching 14 disks. Meta's blob store needs it both fast and cheap. How?
title: Tectonic blobs: replicate now, encode later
body: Blob storage needs low latency for small writes. Encoding every append into RS(10,4) would cost 14 I/Os for a few kilobytes. So the client does a replicated **quorum append**: write to replicas and acknowledge once a quorum has the data. After the block is sealed, the client re-encodes it to RS(10,4) with one large I/O on each of 14 nodes. Azure uses the same pattern.
takeaway: Pay for replication on the hot tail, erasure codes on the cold bulk.
deeper:
**Hedged writes:** The client can send to more nodes than it needs and take the fastest acknowledgments. One slow disk no longer sets the write's latency. Quorum acks and hedging both attack tail latency, the slowest requests that users actually feel.

**The economics:** Many small replicated writes become 14 large ones once the block seals. Blob storage's effective replication reached about 2.8×, versus Haystack's 5.3×.

**Coarse isolation:** Performance isolation is managed across tens of traffic groups with similar latency needs, not hundreds of applications. That keeps a bulk warehouse job from starving latency-sensitive blob traffic without tracking every app.

**One system, two protocols:** The warehouse encodes in memory; blobs replicate, then encode. Both run on the same disks because each tenant's client picks its own write path.

quiz.q: One of the nodes receiving a Tectonic blob append is having a slow moment. Why doesn't the user notice?
quiz.a: The write is acknowledged once a quorum has it, and hedging sends to extra nodes and takes the fastest acknowledgments. The slow node never sets the latency.

mcq.q: Why does Tectonic's blob path replicate first and re-encode to RS(10,4) only after sealing?
options: Encoding each small append would cost 14 I/Os
RS(10,4) cannot survive a single node loss
Replicated data takes less space than RS(10,4)
Sealed blocks can no longer be replicated
mcq.why: Encoding each small, latency-sensitive append would hit 14 nodes. Replicate for fast quorum acks, then encode once with one large I/O per node.

predict.q: Tectonic's blob store must write small blobs fast, yet store them as RS(10,4). What does it do first?
options: Replicate to a quorum, encode after sealing
Encode each blob across 14 nodes at once
Hold blobs in client RAM until a block fills

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: Meta folded Haystack, f4 and its warehouse HDFS clusters into one file system. What did the bill look like?
title: Tectonic: 10.7B files, 10× fewer warehouse clusters
body: One representative Tectonic cluster held 1,590 PB of capacity, 1,250 PB used (about 70%), 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks on 4,208 storage nodes. Blob storage filled about 49% of the space, the warehouse about 51%. Tectonic served around ten tenants and fully replaced Haystack, f4 and HDFS. Blob storage's effective replication fell to about 2.8×, from Haystack's 5.3×.
takeaway: Pooling pays when the tenants are big enough to cover each other.
deeper:
**The metadata proof:** 10.7 billion files and 15 billion blocks in one cluster. LinkedIn's largest single NameNode held about 1 billion objects. The hash-partitioned ZippyDB layers are what made that jump possible.

**The economics proof:** Going from 5.3× to about 2.8× means roughly half the raw disk for the same blob data. Replicate-then-encode keeps blobs cheap, and on shared disks blob storage no longer strands capacity to get IOPS.

**Sharing both ways:** The warehouse absorbed traffic spikes using blob storage's spare IOPS. The near 50/50 split matters: both tenants are large enough that one's slack meaningfully covers the other.

**Fewer clusters:** Warehouse clusters fell 10× in number. That means fewer systems to upgrade and monitor, and fewer separate pools of spare capacity.

quiz.q: After moving to Tectonic, Meta's warehouse hits a sudden traffic spike. Why can it absorb the spike without new disks?
quiz.a: It shares disks with blob storage, whose spare IOPS cover the spike. On separate systems, that spare capacity would have been stranded where the warehouse couldn't use it.

mcq.q: What happened to blob storage's effective replication factor after moving from Haystack to Tectonic?
options: It fell from 5.3× to about 2.8×
It rose from 3.6× to 5.3×
It fell from 3× to about 1.3×
It stayed at 3× plus RAID-6
mcq.why: Replicate-then-encode with RS(10,4) on shared disks ended Haystack's stranded capacity, roughly halving raw disk per byte of blob data.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: Thousands of GPUs pause at the same moment to save a checkpoint. What storage can catch it?
title: Meta's 24,576-GPU clusters checkpoint into Tectonic
body:
Large-model training has one brutal storage moment: every GPU saves its piece of the model state at once, and all of them read it back after a failure. While storage absorbs the burst, GPUs sit idle.

In 2024, Meta said its 24,576-GPU GenAI clusters use a **FUSE** API backed by a flash-optimized version of Tectonic. Thousands of GPUs save and load checkpoints together through ordinary file operations.
takeaway: In training, slow storage bills you in idle GPUs.
deeper:
**Why FUSE:** FUSE lets a user-space file system appear as a normal mounted directory. Training frameworks can checkpoint with standard file APIs instead of a custom client library.

**Why flash:** A checkpoint is a synchronized burst from thousands of ranks (a rank is one training process). Flash sustains that parallel bandwidth far better than hard disks. Meta says optimizing checkpoints cut synchronization to hundreds of milliseconds across thousands of ranks.

**The human side:** Meta also deployed Hammerspace, a parallel NFS system, for interactive developer use. Training jobs get the scalable backend; people get a familiar NFS interface.

**The bigger pattern:** Training looks like HPC: thousands of clients reading and writing in lockstep. That is why parallel file systems and custom flash layers are back in AI clusters.

quiz.q: Your GPU cluster checkpoints every hour and each checkpoint takes minutes. What are you really losing, and what did Meta do about it?
quiz.a: Idle GPU time: every GPU waits while storage absorbs the burst. Meta checkpoints through a flash-optimized Tectonic behind FUSE and says synchronization dropped to hundreds of milliseconds.

mcq.q: What does FUSE give Meta's training code when it checkpoints to Tectonic?
options: A mounted directory usable with ordinary file operations
Direct RDMA access to each disk's raw blocks
Parallel NFS semantics for interactive users
Automatic erasure coding inside the GPU driver
mcq.why: FUSE exposes a user-space file system as a normal mount, so frameworks save and load checkpoints with standard file APIs.

section: Meta Tectonic: one exabyte-scale file system for everything (FAST 2021)
hook: Merging storage systems looks like free money on a spreadsheet. What turns it into an outage instead?
title: Consolidation needs isolation and escape hatches
body:
Specialized systems strand IOPS in one place and capacity in another. One shared multi-tenant layer can reclaim that waste: Meta's blob replication fell from 5.3× to about 2.8× on Tectonic.

But pooling wins only with two extras: **isolation**, like Tectonic's traffic groups, and tenant-specific **escape hatches**, like client-side encoding. Without them, consolidation creates noisy-neighbor outages, where one tenant's burst degrades everyone sharing the disks.
takeaway: Pooling makes the savings. Isolation and escape hatches decide whether you keep them.
deeper:
**Without isolation:** A big warehouse scan can saturate disks and push blob latency past what users tolerate. Tectonic manages performance across tens of traffic groups with similar latency needs, not hundreds of applications, which keeps prioritization manageable.

**Without escape hatches:** One write path forces a compromise on everyone. Either the warehouse pays replication costs or blob storage pays encoding latency. Client-side encoding lets each tenant keep what made its old specialized system good.

**In a design review:** When someone proposes merging storage systems, ask three questions.
1. Which resource is stranded today, and who holds the spare?
2. What stops one tenant from starving another?
3. Which tenant loses its special write path, and what does that cost?

**The tell:** If nobody can answer the second question, the savings are only on paper.

quiz.q: Your team wants to put a latency-critical key-value store and a nightly batch pipeline on one shared disk pool. What two things must the design include?
quiz.a: Performance isolation, so batch bursts can't starve latency-critical traffic, and per-tenant escape hatches, so each workload keeps its own write path instead of a one-size compromise.

mcq.q: What most often turns storage consolidation into noisy-neighbor outages?
options: Pooling tenants without isolation or escape hatches
Using hash partitioning for shared metadata
Running more than ten tenants per cluster
Erasure coding data after it is sealed
mcq.why: Shared disks save money only if one tenant's burst is contained (isolation) and each tenant can keep its own write path (escape hatches).

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
hook: Azure didn't build one giant storage cluster. It built many capped ones. Why cap yourself?
title: Azure grows by adding stamps of 10 to 20 racks
body: Windows Azure Storage (WAS) runs Azure Blobs, Tables and Queues, with strong consistency from the start. Instead of one ever-growing cluster, it adds **storage stamps**: clusters of 10 to 20 racks with 18 disk-heavy storage nodes per rack. First-generation stamps held about 2 PB raw; next-generation stamps up to 30 PB. In 2011, WAS had 70 PB of raw storage in production.
takeaway: Cap the unit, then scale by adding units.
deeper:
**The routing layer:** A Location Service sits above the stamps. It assigns customer accounts to stamps and migrates accounts when a stamp reaches about 70% utilization, so no stamp runs full.

**Why a cap helps:** No stamp exceeds a known size, so everything inside it, metadata included, can be sized for that ceiling. A 30 PB stamp with 1 GB extents has about 30 million extents to track, which fits in memory. Growth beyond that comes from routing accounts, not from stretching one metadata service.

**The headroom:** Migrating at about 70% leaves room inside each stamp for failures, growth and rebalancing.

**Consistency from day one:** GFS left duplicates and padding for applications to clean up. WAS, described in its 2011 SOSP paper, was designed with strong consistency from the start.

quiz.q: An Azure stamp passes 70% utilization while customers keep writing. What happens, and why not just let it fill?
quiz.a: The Location Service migrates some accounts to other stamps. That keeps headroom and keeps each stamp within the size its internal metadata was designed for.

mcq.q: How does Windows Azure Storage grow past one stamp's capacity?
options: A Location Service assigns and migrates accounts across stamps
Each stamp's Stream Manager adds more Paxos replicas
Stamps merge into one cluster at 70% utilization
Partition servers stretch across every rack worldwide
mcq.why: Stamps are capped clusters. The Location Service assigns accounts to stamps and migrates them when a stamp reaches about 70% utilization.

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
hook: Azure makes each write wait for copies in the same stamp, but not for the copy in another region. Why?
title: Azure replicates in sync locally, lazily across regions
body: Each Azure stamp has three layers. Stateless front-ends authenticate and route requests. The **partition layer** understands Blobs, Tables and Queues, range-partitions objects across partition servers, and replicates between stamps asynchronously. The **stream layer** is the distributed file system: it stores bits and replicates inside the stamp synchronously. Local copies protect every write; waiting on a distant stamp every time would add large latency.
takeaway: Replicate synchronously where it's cheap, asynchronously where it's far.
deeper:
**Inside the stamp:** The stream layer acknowledges a write only after its replicas have it. That gives strong consistency and survives disk and node failures within the stamp.

**Between stamps:** The partition layer handles inter-stamp (geo) replication asynchronously. The write path stays fast, and another stamp still holds a copy for disasters, just slightly behind.

**A deliberately dumb bottom:** The stream layer never knows what a blob or table is. It deals only in streams and extents, large append-only units, which keeps its metadata small. The partition layer knows which object sits at which offset of which extent.

**Split by kind:** Object-level metadata lives in the partition layer, storage-level metadata in the stream layer. Each scales on its own: Azure splits metadata by kind, not only by key.

quiz.q: A disaster wipes out an Azure stamp seconds after a write was acknowledged. Is that write guaranteed to exist in another stamp?
quiz.a: No. The acknowledgment waited only for synchronous replicas inside the stamp. Geo-replication to another stamp is asynchronous, so the newest writes may not have arrived yet.

mcq.q: Which Azure layer understands blobs and replicates data between stamps?
options: The partition layer
The stream layer
The front-end layer
The Location Service
mcq.why: The partition layer knows Blobs, Tables and Queues and does async inter-stamp replication. The stream layer only stores bits and replicates within a stamp.

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
hook: Azure lets you append to exactly one piece of each stream. Everything older is frozen for good. Why freeze it?
title: Azure streams: append to the tail, freeze the rest
body: In Azure's stream layer, a **stream** looks like one big append-only file. Underneath, it is an ordered list of pointers to **extents**: sequences of appended blocks with a 1 GB target size, each packing many small objects. Only the last extent can be appended to. Earlier extents are **sealed** and immutable. A Paxos-replicated Stream Manager tracks streams and extents, and Extent Nodes store the replicas.
takeaway: Data that can never change is data you can copy, move and encode freely.
deeper:
**Why freeze:** An immutable extent has no concurrent writer to invalidate a copy. That makes it easy to replicate, cache, move and erasure code. Azure erasure codes sealed extents and then drops the full replicas.

**Small files, solved:** Packing many small objects into 1 GB extents means the stream layer sees a modest number of big units, not billions of tiny objects.

**No single point of failure:** The Stream Manager is Paxos-replicated, so losing one replica loses neither metadata nor availability.

**GFS, fixed:** The design shares GFS's instincts, appends, large units and a central manager, but drops its weak spots. Consistency is strong, the manager is replicated, and it tracks far fewer, larger units. Colossus and Tectonic share the same append-only instinct.

quiz.q: Why is it safe for Azure to erasure code an extent in the background and delete its replicas, but not the extent currently taking appends?
quiz.a: A sealed extent never changes, so its encoded form stays valid. The active tail still receives appends, which would invalidate any encoding, so it stays replicated.

mcq.q: In Azure's stream layer, which extent of a stream can still be appended to?
options: Only the last extent
Any extent under 1 GB
Every extent, in order
Only the first extent
mcq.why: Only the stream's final extent accepts appends. Earlier extents are sealed and immutable, which lets them be erasure coded safely.

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
hook: A 30 PB Azure stamp is packed with small objects, yet its core metadata fits in memory. How?
title: 30 PB, 30 million extents: Azure's metadata stays small
body: The Stream Manager tracks only extents, never individual objects. With 1 GB extents, a 30 PB stamp has about 30 million of them before replication, which fits in memory. The fine-grained index, which blob sits at which offset of which extent, lives in the range-partitioned partition layer, spread across many partition servers. Azure splits metadata by kind: big units at the bottom, small objects elsewhere.

stat.label: extents tracked in a 30 PB stamp

takeaway: Make the bottom layer's units huge and its metadata stays tiny.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** 30 PB divided by 1 GB is about 30 million. Assume a few hundred bytes per extent and that is gigabytes, not terabytes, for one Paxos-replicated service to hold.

**Contrast with HDFS:** A NameNode tracks every file and every block in one heap, so billions of small files mean billions of objects on one machine. Azure's stream layer never sees objects at all.

**The cost:** You still need a second scalable index to find objects. That is the partition layer's job, and it can split and rebalance ranges across servers as load shifts.

**The pattern:** Big units, small index elsewhere. Rather than forcing one metadata service to scale to everything, shrink its job and hand the per-object detail to a layer built for it.

quiz.q: A 30 PB stamp is rebuilt with 1 MB extents instead of 1 GB. What happens to the Stream Manager?
quiz.a: It must track about 30 billion extents instead of 30 million, 1,000× more, which no longer fits comfortably in memory. Big extents are what keep bottom-layer metadata small.

mcq.q: Where does Azure keep the index of which blob sits at which offset of which extent?
options: In the range-partitioned partition layer
In the Paxos-replicated Stream Manager
On each Extent Node's local disk
In the stateless front-end servers
mcq.why: The Stream Manager tracks only extents. The per-object index lives in the partition layer, which scales separately across partition servers.

predict.q: An Azure stamp holds 30 PB. How many items does its Stream Manager track, before replication?
options: About 30 million extents
About 30 billion objects
About 300 billion blocks

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
hook: Rebuilding one lost fragment of a 12-data-fragment code usually means reading 12. Azure reads 6. How?
title: Azure seals, then encodes: 3× down to about 1.3×
body: Active Azure extents keep 3 full replicas, so appends stay fast and simple. Once an extent seals, WAS erasure codes it in the background and deletes the replicas, cutting cost from 3× to about 1.3× to 1.5×. The 2012 follow-up paper introduced **LRC(12,2,2)**, a Local Reconstruction Code: 1.33× overhead, and single-fragment rebuilds read 6 fragments from a local group instead of 12.
takeaway: Replicate what's changing. Encode what's finished.
deeper:
**Local groups:** In LRC(12,2,2), the 12 data fragments form two local groups of 6, each with its own local parity, plus 2 global parities. That is 16 fragments for 12 of data, about 1.33×.

**Why it matters:** Most failures lose a single fragment. LRC rebuilds it from its local group, reading 6 fragments, where a standard Reed-Solomon code with 12 data fragments reads 12. Repair traffic halves and rebuilds finish sooner.

**Where fragments live:** The fragments are spread across 20 fault domains and 10 upgrade domains. Fault domains fail together, like racks. Upgrade domains go down together during planned software rollouts. Data stays readable through both.

**Why seal first:** Only the last extent of each stream is active, so almost all data ends up encoded while writes still hit fast replicas.

quiz.q: A disk holding one fragment of a sealed Azure extent dies. How much does LRC(12,2,2) read to rebuild it, compared with plain Reed-Solomon?
quiz.a: 6 fragments from its local group, versus 12 for a Reed-Solomon code with 12 data fragments. Half the repair traffic, at about 1.33× storage overhead.

mcq.q: When does Azure erasure code an extent?
options: After it is sealed, in the background
On every append, before acknowledging
When its stamp reaches 70% utilization
Only after a replica has been lost
mcq.why: Active extents stay 3× replicated for fast appends. Once sealed and immutable, they are encoded in the background and the full replicas deleted.

section: Microsoft Azure Storage: the stream layer (SOSP 2011)
hook: Azure, Meta and Google each built an exabyte-class storage layer. All three landed on the same three ideas.
title: Azure, Tectonic and Colossus share three ideas
body: Three companies, three designs, one shared playbook. First, **append-only** storage: data is appended, never overwritten in place. Second, **seal-then-encode**: keep the active tail replicated for fast writes, then erasure code it once it is sealed and immutable. Third, a small, fast metadata service tracks big units, extents or blocks, while a separate layer indexes small objects. Azure's stream layer, Tectonic's blob path and Colossus all do all three.
takeaway: Append, seal, encode, track big units. Then look for what's missing.
deeper:
**Append-only:** No overwrite conflicts. New data only lands at the end, so once a unit closes it can become immutable.

**Seal-then-encode:** It settles the fight between write latency and storage cost. Azure goes from 3× to about 1.3× to 1.5×. Tectonic's blob storage goes from quorum-replicated appends to RS(10,4), reaching about 2.8× effective versus Haystack's 5.3×.

**Big units, small index:** Azure's Stream Manager tracks about 30 million extents for a 30 PB stamp, while the partition layer indexes objects.

**Use it as a checklist:** A missing idea shows where a new design will struggle.
1. Random overwrites? Ask how replicas stay consistent.
2. Encodes at write time? Ask what small writes cost.
3. One service tracks every object? Ask what happens at a billion.

quiz.q: A vendor pitches a storage system that erasure codes every write immediately and tracks each object in one metadata server. Which two questions do you ask?
quiz.a: What does a small write cost when each one is encoded across many nodes? And what happens to that single metadata server at a billion objects?

mcq.q: What does seal-then-encode mean in Azure, Tectonic and Colossus?
options: Replicate the active tail, erasure code it once immutable
Encrypt data at rest, then compress each sealed unit
Erasure code every write, then replicate cold data
Seal the metadata log, then rebuild pages from it
mcq.why: Writes land on fast replicas. Once a unit seals and can never change, it is erasure coded to cut storage cost.

hook: Most distributed file systems keep a giant table of where every block lives. Ceph threw that table away.
title: Ceph serves block, object and file from one cluster
body: Ceph began as Sage Weil's PhD project at UC Santa Cruz and became the leading open-source unified storage system. One cluster offers block storage (RBD), S3-compatible object storage (RGW) and a file system (CephFS), all on a common core called **RADOS**. Its distinctive move: compute where data lives with a formula instead of storing a location table, removing a big part of the metadata problem.
takeaway: The cheapest metadata is the metadata you compute instead of store.
deeper:
**One cluster, three jobs:** One set of disks can serve virtual machine disks, S3-style applications and shared file systems, instead of three separate systems, each with its own disks. DigitalOcean built its Block Storage product (2016) on Ceph.

**What RADOS does:** Everything below the interfaces: storing objects, replicating or erasure coding them, detecting failures and recovering.

**Where Ceph sits:** GFS put metadata in one machine's RAM. Colossus and Tectonic moved it into a database. Ceph removes block-location metadata entirely by computing placement.

**What remains:** The file system namespace still needs metadata servers, which CephFS adds. But the mapping from data to disks, which grows with every block written, never has to be stored or looked up. The trade-off: when the cluster map changes, some data must move.

quiz.q: A client wants to read an object. In GFS it would ask the master where the chunk lives. What does a Ceph client do instead?
quiz.a: It computes the location itself: hash the object name to a placement group, then CRUSH maps that group to OSDs using the cluster map. There is no location table to query.

mcq.q: Which Ceph interface provides S3-compatible object storage?
options: RGW
RBD
CephFS
CRUSH
mcq.why: RGW is the S3-compatible object gateway. RBD serves block devices, CephFS the file system, and CRUSH is the placement function, not an interface.

hook: Ceph has no master that remembers where your object lives. So who keeps the books?
title: Ceph's monitors track the cluster, not your objects
body:
A GFS-style master remembers where every chunk lives, and that table grows with your data. Ceph's core, **RADOS**, avoids it. OSDs (object storage daemons, one per disk) store objects, replicate to peers and recover data themselves. A small cluster of **monitors** holds only the cluster map: which OSDs exist, which are up, and the placement rules.

Objects live in pools, each with its own replication or erasure-coding setting. Each object hashes to a **placement group** (PG), and the PG maps to a set of OSDs.
takeaway: Store the rules, not the locations, and your metadata stays tiny.
deeper:
**What the map holds:** OSDs, whether each is up, and the placement rules. It changes when hardware or rules change, not when you write an object. That is why a small monitor cluster can hold it.

**Why placement groups:** hashing millions of objects into a manageable number of PGs gives Ceph a coarser unit to place and recover. Whole PGs map to OSDs, so recovery reasons about PGs instead of individual objects.

**Why pools:** one cluster can protect different data differently. A pool of virtual machine disks can use replication while a pool of colder objects uses erasure coding.

**The name tells you:** RADOS is the Reliable Autonomic Distributed Object Store. OSDs replicate and recover data themselves rather than waiting for a master to direct every copy. The cluster map is the one thing everyone must agree on.

quiz.q: A Ceph cluster gains 10 billion new objects overnight. How much bigger does the monitors' cluster map get, and why?
quiz.a: Essentially no bigger. The map lists OSDs, their state and placement rules, not object locations. Objects hash to placement groups that map to OSDs, so object count doesn't grow the map.

mcq.q: What does the Ceph monitor cluster store?
options: Which OSDs exist, which are up, and placement rules
A table of every object's OSD locations
The file namespace for CephFS directories
The data blocks of each placement group
mcq.why: Monitors hold only the cluster map. Object locations are computed, directories belong to CephFS metadata servers, and data lives on OSDs.

hook: Ceph clients go straight to the right disks without asking anyone where the data is. How do they know?
title: CRUSH: no lookup table, just a formula
body: A central location table must answer every lookup and store a row for every block. Ceph replaces it with **CRUSH**, a deterministic pseudo-random placement function. Given an object's name and the cluster map, any client computes which OSDs hold it: hash the name to a placement group, then CRUSH maps that PG to an ordered list of OSDs. No central table of block locations exists. The client calculates, then goes straight to the disks.
takeaway: A formula never drifts out of sync, but it never makes exceptions either.
deeper:
**Deterministic:** everyone holding the same cluster map gets the same answer, so clients and OSDs agree without asking each other.

**Pseudo-random:** placement spreads data evenly across OSDs as if chosen at random, but nothing records the choices. They can be recomputed at any time.

**What disappears:** GFS keeps chunk locations in master RAM. Tectonic keeps block locations in a Block layer on ZippyDB. Both can put any block anywhere, but must store and scale that mapping. Ceph has no block-location table at all, so there is no location lookup on the data path to overload.

**The catch:** the answer depends on the map. When a disk is added or fails, the output changes for some placement groups, and their data must move. The freedom to place one object by hand is gone too.

quiz.q: Two Ceph clients on opposite sides of a datacenter look up the same object at the same instant, and neither contacts a metadata server. Why do they reach the same OSDs?
quiz.a: CRUSH is deterministic. Both hash the object name to the same placement group and run CRUSH on the same cluster map, so both compute the same ordered OSD list.

mcq.q: What metadata does CRUSH let Ceph avoid storing?
options: A block-to-disk location table
The cluster map of OSDs and rules
Per-pool replication settings
The CephFS directory tree
mcq.why: Any client computes placement from the object name and cluster map, so no location table exists. The map, pool settings and CephFS namespace are still stored.

predict.q: How does a Ceph client find which disks hold an object?
options: It computes the location from the name and cluster map
It asks a monitor for the object's location
It queries a metadata server's location table

hook: Tectonic can move one hot block anywhere. In Ceph, moving one hot object means changing rules. Why?
title: When placement is a formula, data moves with the map
body:
CRUSH knows the cluster's physical hierarchy: OSDs, hosts, racks, rows, datacenters. A rule like "3 replicas in 3 different racks" or "SSD OSDs only" is enforced by the function itself, for every client. That is failure-domain thinking turned into a function, with no single point of failure, no bottleneck and no physical limit to scale.

The price comes from the same property. Location is an output of the map. Add or lose a disk and some data must move. Pinning one hot object to a chosen node means changing rules that affect many objects.
takeaway: If location is computed, changing the inputs moves the data.
deeper:
**Why it's safe:** a placement service that picks nodes can forget a failure domain. A CRUSH rule cannot. Replicas land in separate racks, or on the right device class, because the function only produces answers that satisfy the rule.

**The movement cost:**
1. A disk is added or fails.
2. The cluster map changes.
3. CRUSH's output changes for some placement groups.
4. Their data migrates to the newly computed OSDs.

**The control cost:** Tectonic and Colossus record where each block lives, so they can place any block freely. The price is storing and scaling that mapping. Ceph skips the mapping, so it cannot make a one-off exception for a single hot object.

**The trade in one line:** no block-location table at all, in exchange for data that moves when the map changes and less control per object.

quiz.q: One object in your Ceph cluster is read far more than any other. A teammate wants to move just that object to an idle SSD node. What's the problem?
quiz.a: Its location is whatever CRUSH computes from the map and rules. You can't place one object by hand; changing rules or the map shifts placement for many objects and moves their data.

mcq.q: What happens in Ceph when a new disk joins the cluster?
options: The map changes and some data migrates to new OSDs
Nothing moves until a monitor edits a location table
Only newly written objects can land on the new disk
Clients must re-register every object with monitors
mcq.why: Placement is computed from the cluster map, so changing the map changes where some placement groups belong, and their data moves.

hook: For ten years Ceph stored every object as a file on a local file system. Then it walked away. Why?
title: Ceph dropped the local file system after a decade
body:
A local file system looks like a free foundation: someone else already solved disk layout. Ceph's FileStore ran on one for a decade. A SOSP 2019 paper explains why that stopped paying off. Efficient transactions on a file system were very hard, local metadata performance hurt distributed performance, and support for new hardware was slow.

So Ceph built **BlueStore**, which runs on raw devices. It became the default in 2017, and 70% of surveyed users ran it by 2018.
takeaway: A borrowed foundation is free only if your workload plays to its strengths.
deeper:
**What BlueStore added:** full checksums, inline compression and fast overwrites of erasure-coded data. Owning the device let Ceph build the semantics it needed instead of emulating them on top of a file system.

**Why transactions hurt:** Ceph serves block devices and file systems, so it needs fine-grained updates and transactions. Making those efficient on a local file system was the core difficulty the paper describes.

**The counterexample:** Tectonic keeps its chunks on XFS and does fine. Its workload is mostly large, immutable chunks, which local file systems handle well. Same tool, different write pattern, opposite verdict.

**The lesson:** building on a local file system can cost more than it saves. Before you inherit one, check whether your write pattern is what it is good at.

quiz.q: Tectonic stores chunks on XFS happily, yet Ceph left local file systems for raw devices. Resolve the contradiction.
quiz.a: Workload. Tectonic mostly writes large immutable chunks, which file systems handle well. Ceph needs fine-grained updates and transactions, which were very hard to make efficient on a file system.

mcq.q: What did BlueStore change about how Ceph stores objects?
options: It writes directly to raw devices instead of local files
It moved object data into a separate key-value database
It replaced CRUSH with a central location table
It stored objects on XFS instead of another file system
mcq.why: BlueStore runs on raw devices, replacing FileStore's files-on-a-local-file-system design, and added checksums, inline compression and fast erasure-coded overwrites.

predict.q: Why did Ceph stop storing objects as files on a local file system?
options: Efficient transactions on a file system were very hard
Local file systems could not hold enough objects
Local file systems capped disk capacity per node

hook: Ceph computes where every object lives, yet CephFS still runs metadata servers. What's left to store?
title: CRUSH finds the bytes. It can't name your files.
body:
CRUSH answers one question: which OSDs hold this object. A file system needs more: directory trees, file names, and which objects make up each file. That namespace can't be computed, so CephFS adds **metadata servers** (MDS).

Multiple active MDS daemons split the directory tree into **subtrees**. Admins can pin subtrees to specific MDS ranks, or use ephemeral pinning, which hashes directories across ranks. A dynamic balancer can split and move subtrees to less loaded ranks.
takeaway: Computing placement removes one kind of metadata, never all of it.
deeper:
**Why subtrees:** one MDS owns a whole part of the tree, so listing or creating files in a directory stays on one server. That locality is the strength of subtree partitioning.

**The weakness:** a hot subtree can overload the one MDS that owns it, and balancing is hard. Lustre DNE, which lets multiple metadata targets split its namespace, belongs to the same family and shares the problem.

**Three ways to balance:**
1. Static pinning: an admin assigns subtrees to ranks. Predictable, but needs a human.
2. Ephemeral pinning: directories are hashed across ranks for even load, at some cost to locality.
3. Dynamic balancer: splits and moves subtrees to less loaded ranks automatically.

**The bigger point:** Ceph removed block-location metadata with a formula, and the namespace still needed its own scaling plan.

quiz.q: One CephFS directory tree full of a busy team's scratch files is overloading its MDS while other ranks sit idle. What are your options?
quiz.a: Pin the hot subtree to a quieter rank, turn on ephemeral pinning to hash its directories across ranks, or let the dynamic balancer split and move the subtree.

mcq.q: Why does CephFS still need metadata servers?
options: CRUSH locates objects but not names or directories
CRUSH cannot place objects across different racks
Monitors are too slow to serve object reads
OSDs cannot replicate data without an MDS
mcq.why: Names, directories and file-to-object mappings can't be computed, so MDS daemons store and serve them. CRUSH only answers where object data lives.

hook: A cloud provider needed disks for customer VMs and chose not to write its own storage system. What did it run?
title: DigitalOcean and CERN run storage they didn't build
body:
Google and Meta write their own file systems. Most organizations don't. DigitalOcean built its Block Storage product in 2016 on Ceph: all-SSD, with 3 replicas across separate servers and racks. CERN has run Ceph for about a decade and presented a "10 years retrospective" in 2023.

What Ceph gives them: an open-source, self-healing cluster offering block (**RBD**), object and file interfaces, with no central table of object locations to outgrow.
takeaway: Write the failure domain into the placement rule, and every copy obeys it.
deeper:
**Why it fits block storage:** RBD gives virtual machines their disks. DigitalOcean's layout, 3 replicas on separate servers and racks, is exactly the kind of rule CRUSH expresses directly. Every replica respects the failure domain without a placement service deciding each time.

**Why a decade matters:** running one storage system for ten years means living through hardware generations and growth. In Ceph, new hardware changes the cluster map and data rebalances automatically. That rebalancing is also the bill: data moves whenever the map changes.

**Who this is for:** organizations that run storage built by others rather than writing their own. For them, the draw is open source, one cluster for block, object and file, and no location table on the data path.

quiz.q: You're building VM block storage on Ceph and must survive a whole rack failing. How would a layout like DigitalOcean's guarantee that?
quiz.a: A CRUSH rule placing 3 replicas on separate servers in separate racks. Every client computes placement from that rule, so losing one rack never takes every copy.

mcq.q: How was DigitalOcean's 2016 Block Storage built on Ceph?
options: All-SSD, 3 replicas across separate servers and racks
All-HDD, RS(6,3) erasure coding within one rack
SSD cache over HDD, 2 replicas on one server
All-SSD, LRC(12,2,2) across three datacenters
mcq.why: DigitalOcean chose all-SSD with 3 replicas spread over separate servers and racks, so a single server or rack failure never takes every copy.

section: Lustre and GPFS: HPC and AI training
hook: Thousands of processes need the same enormous file at once, and one server can't feed them. What can?
title: Lustre splits one file across many servers
body: HPC differs from web workloads: thousands of compute nodes read and write the same huge files in parallel, with strict POSIX semantics, over fast networks like InfiniBand. One server's bandwidth is a hard ceiling. Lustre breaks it with **striping**: one file is spread across many object storage targets (**OSTs**). A kernel client fetches the layout from a metadata target (MDT), then reads and writes many OSTs directly, so one file gets many servers' bandwidth.
takeaway: When one file outgrows one server, split the file, not the workload.
deeper:
**The parts:** a management server (MGS); metadata servers and targets (MDS/MDT) holding the namespace and file layouts; object storage servers and targets (OSS/OST) holding data.

**A familiar shape:** fetch the layout from the metadata service once, then talk to storage directly. GFS clients do the same with chunk locations. The difference is the interface: Lustre's kernel clients give applications strict POSIX, while GFS and HDFS use custom, non-POSIX interfaces.

**Scaling metadata:** DNE (Distributed Namespace) lets multiple MDTs split the namespace. Even so, the Tectonic paper notes that Lustre limits the number of metadata nodes, which limits scalability.

**At scale:** Oak Ridge's Frontier supercomputer uses Orion, a Lustre file system on HPE ClusterStor with 679 PB of usable namespace and separate performance and capacity OST pools.

quiz.q: A simulation's 1,000 processes each read their own slice of one huge input file, and throughput is stuck at one server's bandwidth. What Lustre feature fixes it, and how?
quiz.a: Striping the file across many OSTs. After fetching the layout from the MDT, each process reads its slice directly from different OSTs, so the file gets many servers' bandwidth.

mcq.q: In Lustre, where does a client get a file's layout before reading data?
options: From the metadata target (MDT)
From the management server (MGS)
From each object storage target (OST)
From a CRUSH computation on the client
mcq.why: The MDT holds the namespace and file layouts. With the layout in hand, the client reads and writes the OSTs directly.

section: Lustre and GPFS: HPC and AI training
hook: A file system that feeds a supercomputer at 2.5 TB/s can still be the wrong pick for a web company. Why?
title: Built for a few giant files, not billions of small ones
body:
Summit, Oak Ridge's previous flagship, used a 250 PB GPFS file system with 2.5 TB/s of bandwidth. GPFS is IBM's parallel file system, widely used in HPC and enterprise. Lustre and GPFS are tuned for high-throughput parallel access to a few enormous files.

A web company's warehouse or blob store looks different: billions of files, many small, so metadata becomes the pressure point. The Tectonic paper names the weak spot: Lustre limits the number of **metadata nodes**, which limits scalability.
takeaway: Ask what's scarce: bandwidth to one file, or metadata for a billion.
deeper:
**What HPC optimizes:** a simulation might have thousands of processes writing one checkpoint or a few huge output files. Metadata operations are few. Bandwidth is everything, so striping and fast networks win.

**What web scale needs:** billions of files. LinkedIn runs about 1 billion objects on a single HDFS NameNode, with peak load of 250K operations per second. That is a metadata problem first, and a design with few metadata nodes hits its limit.

**How GPFS differs:** it uses distributed metadata with distributed locking rather than dedicated metadata targets, and protects data with RAID or replication. Both GPFS and Lustre present POSIX.

**The calibration:** Summit's 2.5 TB/s is bandwidth for parallel HPC jobs. Colossus regularly exceeds 50 TB/s read, serving services like Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery. Different workloads, different targets.

quiz.q: Your team wants to host a photo service with billions of small files on the Lustre cluster your research group already owns. What's the risk?
quiz.a: Lustre is tuned for bandwidth to a few enormous files and limits the number of metadata nodes. Billions of small files make metadata the bottleneck, which that design scales poorly.

mcq.q: Which limit makes Lustre a weak fit for billions of small files?
options: It limits the number of metadata nodes
It caps each stripe at 64 MB of data
It cannot run over InfiniBand networks
It lacks POSIX semantics for clients
mcq.why: Billions of files mean heavy metadata load. Lustre limits its metadata nodes, which the Tectonic paper names as its scalability weak point.

section: Lustre and GPFS: HPC and AI training
hook: Supercomputer file systems looked like a niche. Then AI training made them matter again. What changed?
title: AI training made parallel file systems matter again
body:
Large model training looks like HPC. Thousands of GPUs read data in parallel, then write checkpoints at the same moment. A slow checkpoint means idle GPUs, so storage bandwidth turns into compute time.

That is why AI clusters use parallel file systems or custom flash layers. Meta's 2024 GenAI clusters combine a flash-optimized Tectonic behind **FUSE** with Hammerspace NFS. Meta says optimizing checkpoints cut synchronization to hundreds of milliseconds across thousands of **ranks**.
takeaway: In synchronized training, the slowest storage write sets everyone's pace.
deeper:
**Two phases, two patterns:**
1. Reading: many GPUs each stream their share of the dataset, often again every epoch.
2. Checkpointing: every rank (training process) saves state at once, and the job waits for the slowest.

**Why the tail costs GPUs:** during a synchronized checkpoint, one straggling write holds up the whole job. Storage delay turns directly into idle accelerators.

**Why the old tools fit:** this is what Lustre and GPFS were built for: bandwidth to large files, parallel access, and POSIX interfaces that frameworks already use.

**How Meta adapted:** a version of Tectonic optimized for flash sits behind a FUSE API, so standard file code works and thousands of GPUs can save and load checkpoints together. Hammerspace (parallel NFS) serves interactive developer use.

quiz.q: Your training job checkpoints every hour and storage is fast on average, yet GPU utilization collapses at every checkpoint. What's going on?
quiz.a: Checkpoints are synchronized: every rank writes at once and the job waits for the slowest write. The average doesn't matter, the tail does, and all GPUs idle until it lands.

mcq.q: Why does a slow checkpoint hurt a large training job so much?
options: Every rank waits, so all the GPUs sit idle
It blocks reads of training data from the object store
The scheduler kills jobs that checkpoint slowly
GPU memory is freed only after a checkpoint ends
mcq.why: Checkpoints are synchronized: every rank saves at once and the job waits for the slowest write, so storage delay becomes idle GPU time.

hook: Take a Redis instance, add an object store bucket, and you get a POSIX file system. What does each half do?
title: JuiceFS: a database for names, an object store for bytes
body: Object storage is cheap and durable but slow, and it doesn't behave like a file system. **JuiceFS** puts a file system facade with caching on top. Metadata lives in an engine you choose: Redis, TiKV, MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQLite. Data goes to any object store, split into chunks (up to 64 MB), slices, and blocks (default up to 4 MB) uploaded in parallel. Clients connect through FUSE, a Hadoop SDK, Kubernetes CSI or an S3 gateway, with local caching.
takeaway: Metadata in a database is no longer a hyperscaler's secret.
deeper:
**The lineage:** Colossus stores metadata in Bigtable. Tectonic uses ZippyDB. JuiceFS packages the same idea for anyone with an object store: bring your own database.

**Why split it:** a database answers small metadata queries quickly. An object store holds bulk data cheaply and durably. Local caching hides the object store's latency. Each component does what it is good at.

**Why the block hierarchy:** files break into chunks, slices and blocks, and blocks upload in parallel for throughput. The metadata engine records which pieces make up each file.

**The catch:** durability now has two owners. Every block can be safe in the object store while the file system is gone, if the metadata engine loses its state. Choose the engine as carefully as the bucket.

quiz.q: Your team runs JuiceFS for ML data. Reading hot files is fast, but listing a huge directory is slow. Which component do you look at first, and why?
quiz.a: The metadata engine. Directory listings are metadata operations served by Redis, TiKV or the SQL database, not by the object store, so the engine decides their speed.

mcq.q: Where does JuiceFS keep file system metadata?
options: In an engine you pick, like Redis, TiKV or MySQL
In the object store alongside the data blocks
In one in-memory master, like a NameNode
Only in each client's local cache
mcq.why: JuiceFS stores metadata in a database engine you choose and data in any object store: the Colossus and Tectonic pattern, packaged for anyone.

hook: Every training epoch re-reads the same dataset from a remote object store. Why pay for that trip every time?
title: Alluxio keeps hot data next to the GPUs
body: Compute and storage often live apart: GPUs in one cluster, data in a cloud object store or remote HDFS, so every read crosses the network. **Alluxio**, from UC Berkeley's AMPLab and originally called Tachyon, sits in between as a data orchestration and caching layer. It mounts backends like S3, GCS, HDFS, NFS, Ceph and Alibaba OSS under one namespace, and caches hot data across memory, SSD and HDD tiers. A common use: keeping remote training data near GPUs, so repeated epochs skip the object store.
takeaway: A cache buys speed and one namespace, never durability.
deeper:
**Why epochs love caches:** training reads the same dataset again every epoch. The first pass warms the cache near the GPUs, and later passes read locally instead of re-fetching from the object store.

**One tree, many stores:** applications see a single namespace even though data sits in S3, GCS, HDFS or Ceph underneath. HDFS ViewFs does something similar for several NameNode namespaces.

**Tiers by heat:** memory holds the hottest data, SSD the warm, HDD larger cached sets.

**The boundary:** Alluxio caches are, by design, not the source of truth. The underlying stores own durability. Losing the cache costs speed, as long as writes reached the store underneath. Trouble starts when a team treats cached content as if it were stored.

quiz.q: An Alluxio worker dies mid-training. Assuming all writes went to the underlying store, what did the job lose?
quiz.a: Only cached copies, so some speed while the cache rewarms. The underlying stores are the source of truth and still hold every byte.

mcq.q: What is Alluxio's role between compute and storage?
options: A cache with one namespace over many backends
The durable system of record for training data
An object store that replaces S3 and GCS
A metadata engine for JuiceFS file systems
mcq.why: Alluxio mounts backends like S3, HDFS and Ceph under one namespace and caches hot data in tiers. The backends remain the source of truth.

hook: Every data block is safe in S3, yet the whole file system is gone. How?
title: Safe blocks, lost file system: the metadata trap
body:
The mistake is treating a caching layer as the system of record. JuiceFS's durability depends on two things: the object store and the metadata engine. Run that engine on a single Redis without persistence, and you can lose the map from files to blocks. Every block survives in S3, but nothing says which blocks form which file, in what order, under which directory.

Alluxio is simpler: its caches are, by design, not the source of truth.
takeaway: A system is exactly as durable as its least durable required part.
deeper:
**Why blocks alone are useless:** an object store full of blocks without their metadata is a pile of anonymous fragments. The mapping from names to files to blocks is what turns them into data.

**The fix:** give the metadata engine at least the durability of the data store. That means persistence and replication, not a single in-memory instance.

**For Alluxio:** writes must reach the underlying store. Then losing the cache costs performance, not data. Problems start when a team writes only to the cache layer or assumes cached content is durable.

**The general version:** many "data" outages are really metadata outages. When you review a layered storage stack, trace where each piece of state lives and what actually protects it.

quiz.q: A startup runs JuiceFS on S3 with one Redis node, persistence off, to save money. The Redis host reboots. What do they have afterwards?
quiz.a: An S3 bucket full of intact blocks and no file system. The file-to-block mapping and directory tree lived only in Redis memory, so nothing can reassemble the files.

mcq.q: What must be true for a JuiceFS deployment to be durable?
options: Both the object store and metadata engine are durable
The object store alone is durable and replicated
Every client's local cache is backed up nightly
Data blocks are kept at or under 4 MB each
mcq.why: JuiceFS needs both halves. Blocks in the object store are meaningless if the metadata engine that maps files to blocks loses its state.

predict.q: Every JuiceFS data block is safely stored in S3. Can you still lose the file system?
options: Yes, if the metadata engine loses its state
No, S3 holds everything needed to rebuild it
Only if S3 itself loses some objects

hook: HDFS never gave up on a central master. Three tricks stretched it anyway. What were they?
title: Three ways to stretch a single master before it snaps
body: Every system here scales data by adding servers. Metadata is the hard part, and the first three approaches keep a central master. A **single in-memory master** (GFS, early HDFS) is simple, fast and strongly consistent, but capped by RAM, CPU and recovery time. **Static partitioning** (HDFS Federation) runs several masters, each owning part of the tree. **Read replicas** (Observer NameNode) serve reads from followers, while writes still hit one node.
takeaway: Incremental fixes postpone the metadata ceiling; they don't remove it.
deeper:
**Single master:** all metadata in one server's RAM, plus an operation log. Strong semantics and simple code. Its limits are RAM, CPU and recovery time.

**Static partitioning:** independent masters joined by ViewFs mount tables or routers. The costs: manual balancing, hot directories stay hot, and moving data across namespaces is a copy, not a rename.

**Read replicas:** followers tail the log and serve reads. Because most operations are reads, the win is big. LinkedIn reports reads at about 95% of operations, and LinkedIn and Uber both adopted the Observer NameNode. The price is a state-ID consistency protocol so clients don't read stale data.

**Why HDFS took this path:** each step keeps the familiar single-master code and adds capacity around it. Writes, and each namespace's memory, stay bound to single processes.

quiz.q: Your NameNode is overloaded and 95% of its traffic is reads. A teammate proposes Federation; you propose Observers. Which helps more, and why?
quiz.a: Observers. They absorb the reads, which are nearly all the load, without splitting the tree. Federation means deciding which directories go where, and a hot directory stays hot on its NameNode.

mcq.q: What limit remains after adding HDFS Observer NameNodes?
options: All writes still go to one active NameNode
Reads must still go to the active NameNode
Cross-namespace moves become full copies
Block reports stop reaching the NameNodes
mcq.why: Observers serve reads from the tailed edit log, but every write still goes through the single active NameNode. Full-copy moves are a Federation cost.

hook: Give up on one master and you have at least five ways to spread metadata. Each one breaks something.
title: Five ways past the single master, and what each costs
body: Once metadata leaves one machine, each design pays a different price. **Metadata in a distributed database** (Colossus on Bigtable, Tectonic on ZippyDB, JuiceFS) scales to billions of files, but cross-shard renames are hard. **Layering by kind** (Tectonic, ADLS, Azure) lets each layer scale separately, at the cost of more RPC hops. **Computed placement** (Ceph CRUSH) drops the location table, but data moves when the map changes. Big units with an index elsewhere (Azure) keep bottom metadata tiny. Subtree partitioning (CephFS, Lustre DNE) keeps directory locality.
takeaway: Every metadata design moves the pain; choose which operation gets to be slow.
deeper:
**Distributed database:** namespace and block maps become rows in a sharded database. Strength: billions of files and exabytes. Weakness: rename across shards is hard, and you inherit the database's behavior.

**Layered by kind:** separate layers for names, files and blocks, or for extents versus objects. Tectonic hash-partitions its layers, ADLS range-partitions, and Azure splits the stream layer from the partition layer. More moving parts, more hops.

**Formulas and big units:** CRUSH needs no block-location table but gives up per-object control. Azure's stream layer tracks 1 GB extents, which keeps its metadata tiny but needs a second scalable layer to index objects.

**Subtrees, and mixing:** metadata servers own parts of the tree and get rebalanced: good locality, hard balancing, hot subtrees. Real systems combine approaches. Tectonic is database-backed and layered. Ceph pairs CRUSH with subtree-partitioned MDS.

quiz.q: Your product's users constantly rename and move large directory trees. Which metadata design should worry you most, and why?
quiz.a: Hash-partitioned or database-backed metadata. A tree's entries scatter across shards, so a rename or move becomes a hard cross-shard operation. Subtree partitioning keeps a directory's metadata together.

mcq.q: What is the main weakness of computing placement, as Ceph's CRUSH does?
options: Data moves when the cluster map changes
Cross-shard renames need distributed locks
Every lookup adds an extra RPC hop
A second layer must index every object
mcq.why: Placement is a function of the cluster map, so any map change moves data. The other options are costs of databases, layering and big-unit designs.

hook: The disks are healthy and every byte is intact, yet the service is down. Where should you have looked first?
title: Many data outages are really metadata outages
body:
When you review a storage design, find the metadata path first. Four questions expose it. How many metadata objects per PB? What is the read/write ratio of metadata operations? Which operations are **cross-shard**: rename, listing a huge directory, deleting a tree? How long does metadata recovery take after a crash?

Often the bytes are fine. When metadata is slow or lost, the data is still there and nobody can find it.
takeaway: Before you count the disks, count the metadata objects.
deeper:
**Objects per PB:** Shvachko's rule of thumb is about 1 GB of NameNode metadata per PB of storage, at average file sizes. Small files break it; LinkedIn and Uber hit namespace limits before the disks filled.

**Read/write ratio:** reads were about 95% of LinkedIn's NameNode operations, which made Observer NameNodes a big win. Write-heavy metadata wouldn't benefit the same way.

**Cross-shard operations:** in hash-partitioned or database-backed metadata, a rename or tree delete touches many shards. Know which operations your users depend on.

**Recovery time:** a GFS master must load its checkpoint and replay its log while writes stop. An HDFS standby must read all edits before becoming active. JuiceFS on a non-persistent Redis shows the extreme: blocks safe in S3, file system gone.

quiz.q: A design review shows a new blob store with 10× more metadata writes than reads. Why is "add read replicas" the wrong first answer?
quiz.a: Read replicas only offload reads; every write still goes to one node. With writes dominating, the metadata path needs partitioning or a distributed design, not followers.

mcq.q: Which operation is typically hardest in hash-partitioned metadata?
options: Renaming a directory tree across shards
Reading one file's list of blocks
Looking up a single file's entry
Appending to a file's last block
mcq.why: Hashing scatters a tree's entries across shards, so a rename or tree delete becomes a cross-shard operation. Single-entry lookups stay cheap.

hook: Ten file systems, ten designs. One column in the comparison separates them more than any other. Which?
title: Ten file systems compared: metadata is the real divide
body: Line up GFS, Colossus, HDFS, Tectonic, Azure's stream layer, Ceph, Lustre, GPFS, JuiceFS and Alluxio. Units run from 4 MB JuiceFS blocks to 1 GB Azure extents. Redundancy drifts from 3× replication toward erasure coding, often applied after data seals. Interfaces split into custom append-only or write-once APIs (GFS, Colossus, Tectonic, Azure, HDFS) and **POSIX** (Lustre, GPFS, JuiceFS, Alluxio). The column that truly separates them is **metadata design**: one master's RAM, a database, layers, a formula, or a namespace over other stores.
takeaway: Compare storage systems by metadata design first; everything else follows from it.
deeper:
**Published scale:** GFS 1,000+ nodes and 300+ TB (2003). Colossus: two file systems over 10 EB each (2025). HDFS at LinkedIn: 500 PB in one cluster, 1 EB total (2021). Tectonic: a 1,590 PB cluster with 10.7B files (2021). Azure: 70 PB raw (2011), stamps up to 30 PB. Lustre: 679 PB Orion at Frontier. GPFS: 250 PB and 2.5 TB/s at Summit.

**Consistency:** GFS is relaxed (defined vs consistent). HDFS is single writer with strong metadata. Tectonic is single writer per file with linearizable metadata. Azure is strong, and so is RADOS. Lustre and GPFS are POSIX. Colossus's model is not fully published.

**Redundancy:** GFS 3× replication. Colossus mixes replication and Reed-Solomon via client RAID. Tectonic picks per tenant: RS(9,6), RS(3,3), or replicated then RS(10,4). Azure goes 3× then LRC(12,2,2). Lustre usually relies on hardware RAID under OSTs. JuiceFS and Alluxio delegate redundancy to their backends.

quiz.q: A vendor pitches you a new distributed file system. Which single question about it tells you most about how it will scale?
quiz.a: How it stores and scales metadata: one master in RAM, a sharded database, layers, computed placement, or another system's namespace. Every data path scales by adding servers; metadata is where designs diverge.

mcq.q: Which systems in the comparison offer POSIX interfaces?
options: Lustre, GPFS, JuiceFS and Alluxio
GFS, HDFS, Colossus and Tectonic
Azure streams, Ceph RADOS and GFS
Tectonic, Colossus, Lustre and HDFS
mcq.why: Lustre and GPFS are POSIX HPC file systems, and JuiceFS and Alluxio offer POSIX among their interfaces. GFS, HDFS, Colossus and Tectonic use custom APIs.

hook: Every distributed file system since 2003 is an answer to the same question. Can you name it?
title: The data path scales. The metadata path is the story.
body: Add storage servers and the data path scales almost linearly. The metadata path does not, and each DFS generation is a new answer to it. GFS (2003) put everything in one master's RAM, and that master became the limit. HDFS copied GFS, then added federation, QJM-based HA, Observer NameNodes and striped EC. Colossus moved metadata into Bigtable and scales over 100× past GFS. Tectonic split metadata into hash-partitioned layers. Azure tracks 1 GB extents. Ceph computes placement instead of storing it.
takeaway: Find the metadata path and you've found the design's ceiling.
deeper:
**The numbers to keep:** HDFS needs about 600 bytes of NameNode RAM per average file, yet LinkedIn runs 500 PB in one cluster with about 1 billion objects on one NameNode (2021). Two Colossus file systems exceed 10 EB each (2025).

**The patterns to reuse:** Tectonic replaced Haystack, f4 and HDFS with one multi-tenant system where each tenant chooses its encoding. Azure seals 1 GB extents and erasure codes them with LRC, while the object index lives in the partition layer. Append-only storage, seal-then-encode, and a small service tracking big units keep showing up.

**The trade-offs to remember:** CRUSH removes block-location metadata but moves data when the map changes. BlueStore showed that building on local file systems can cost more than it saves. Lustre and GPFS are back for AI training's parallel reads and synchronized checkpoints. JuiceFS and Alluxio add file semantics over object storage, and JuiceFS durability depends on its metadata engine too.

quiz.q: A colleague says their new storage design "scales linearly: just add servers." What follow-up question tests whether that's true?
quiz.a: How does the metadata scale? Adding servers scales the data path. Namespace entries and block maps, and the RAM, CPU and recovery time behind them, are what capped GFS-style designs.

mcq.q: Where did Colossus move file system metadata to escape GFS's limits?
options: Into Bigtable, behind horizontally scaled curators
Into ZippyDB, split into Name, File and Block layers
Into a Paxos-replicated Stream Manager
Into a CRUSH map held by monitors
mcq.why: Colossus curators store metadata in Bigtable, which let it scale over 100× past the largest GFS clusters. ZippyDB is Tectonic, Stream Manager is Azure, CRUSH is Ceph.
